lectures.name: Anatomy of the Kidneys, Ureters, & Adrenal Glands
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Kidneys, Ureters, Bladder and Adrenal Glands
lectures.framing: The kidneys, ureters and adrenal glands are retroperitoneal structures held in place by fat and renal fascia rather than firm attachments. The page runs top to bottom: kidney coverings and hilum, renal vessels (left vs right asymmetry), autonomic supply of kidney vs ureter, then the ureters, bladder and urethra, and the adrenal glands.
lectures.keypoints: Hilum order anterior → posterior: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis. The right renal artery is longer and passes behind the IVC; the left renal vein is longer, passes in front of the aorta but behind the SMA (nutcracker) and receives the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins. Segmental arteries are end arteries. Kidney sympathetics and afferents = T10-L1; ureter = T11-L2 (loin to groin pain); ureter parasympathetics = S2-S4 pelvic splanchnics, kidney = vagus. Stones lodge at the pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim and bladder wall. The uterine artery crosses the ureter (hysterectomy injury). Male urethra has 2 sphincters, female 1 (external).

blocks.html:
Kidneys
  • Retroperitoneal, at T12-L3; the right kidney sits slightly lower because the liver displaces it
  • Supported by extensive fat pads in the paravertebral gutters, with no firm attachment points
  • Renal fascia encloses the kidney, the suprarenal (adrenal) gland and the perirenal fat
    • Perirenal fat lies inside the fascia; pararenal fat lies outside it
  • Renal capsule: fibrous layer on the surface of the kidney
  • Renal hilum, anterior → posterior: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
  • Hydronephrosis: dilatation and distension of the renal pelvis and calyces from obstruction of urine flow (enlarged pelvis and pyramids on ultrasound)

blocks.html:
Ureters
  • Retroperitoneal paired muscular tubes carrying urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder
  • Each ureter enters the bladder obliquely, which acts as a valve against backflow of urine and infection
  • The uterine artery crosses the ureter: risk of ureteric damage during hysterectomy
  • Sites of relative constriction where stones obstruct:
    1. Junction of the renal pelvis and ureter
    2. Crossing the pelvic brim (over the common iliac arteries)
    3. Passage into the bladder wall
  • Ureteric stone symptoms: sharp back or lower abdominal pain (T11-L2 dermatomes, moving down as the stone descends), hematuria, nausea and vomiting
Bladder
  • Distensible, with strong muscular walls (detrusor muscle); has an apex (anterior), fundus (posterior) and neck (inferior)
  • Trigone: smooth triangle on the posterior wall forming a funnel from the ureteric orifices to the urethra
  • Median umbilical ligament supports the apex and is the embryological remnant of the urachus

Adrenal (suprarenal) glands
  • Paired endocrine glands on the superior poles of the kidneys, enclosed in renal fascia and fat, so they stay in place if the kidney is removed
  • Cortex: mesoderm; secretes corticosteroids (cortisol, aldosterone) and androgens
  • Medulla: neural crest cells; secretes catecholamines
  • Right gland: contacts the diaphragm, liver and IVC; vein drains directly into the IVC
  • Left gland: contacts the spleen, stomach, pancreas and diaphragm; vein drains into the left renal vein → IVC
  • Arterial supply from three suprarenal arteries: superior (from the inferior phrenic artery), middle (from the abdominal aorta), inferior (from the renal artery)

lectures.name: Development of the Urinary Tract
lectures.title: Development of the Urinary Tract
lectures.framing: The urinary and genital systems both come from the intermediate mesoderm. The kidney forms as three successive systems (pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros), and the permanent kidney depends on reciprocal induction between the ureteric bud and the metanephrogenic blastema. The page covers kidney development and ascent, then the bladder and urethra from the cloaca, then the congenital anomalies each step explains.
lectures.keypoints: Ureteric bud (from the mesonephric duct) → collecting system (ureter, pelvis, calyces, collecting tubules); metanephrogenic blastema → nephrons. Metanephros starts at week 5, makes urine from ~12 weeks; nephrogenesis ends at birth. Kidneys ascend and rotate medially at weeks 6-9; retained lower vessels = supernumerary (end) arteries. Fetal urine makes amniotic fluid, so no urine → oligohydramnios. Failed reciprocal induction = renal agenesis (bilateral is incompatible with life). Horseshoe kidney (1:500) is caught under the IMA. Urachus remnant = median umbilical ligament; a fully patent one = urachal fistula (urine from the umbilicus).

blocks.html:
Derivatives
  • Urinary and genital systems derive from the intermediate mesoderm
  • Urogenital ridge: longitudinal elevation of intermediate mesoderm beside the aorta, which differentiates into the nephrogenic cord (urinary system) and the gonadal ridge (genital system)

rows: Early week 4 (degenerates by end of week 5)
Functional excretory organ for ~4 weeks (about weeks 6-10)
Regresses at 10-12 weeks as the metanephros takes over; its mesonephric (Wolffian) duct persists and gives rise to the ureteric bud
Develops from the ureteric bud plus the metanephrogenic blastema

blocks.html:
Mesonephros
  • Mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts grow dorsolateral to the nephrogenic cord in a cranial → caudal direction, fuse with the cloaca, then canalize
  • Mesonephric tubules develop within the nephrogenic cord (cranial → caudal) into excretory units resembling the adult nephron: tubules lengthen into an S-shape, a glomerular (Bowman's) capsule forms around a glomerulus, and the tubule fuses with the mesonephric duct to open a passage to the cloaca

rows: Collecting system: ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, millions of collecting tubules (differentiates weeks 5-8)
Repeated branching gives the fetal kidney its lobulated appearance (persistent fetal lobulation if fusion is incomplete, asymptomatic)
Renal vesicles elongate into S-shaped tubules: one end invaginates around a glomerulus as Bowman's capsule (= renal corpuscle), the other forms the PCT, loop of Henle and DCT

blocks.html:
• Reciprocal induction: differentiation of the ureteric bud and the metanephrogenic blastema each depends on contact with the other
  • The kidney becomes functional at ~12 weeks when the distal tubule connects to the collecting ducts
  • Nephrons keep forming until birth; nephrogenesis ends at birth, so nephrons have no regenerative potential
Ascent of the kidneys
  • Kidneys start in the pelvis with the hilum facing ventrally, then ascend and rotate medially between weeks 6-9 (relative ascent as the caudal embryo lengthens), passing through the fork of the umbilical arteries
  • Ascent stops at the (large fetal) adrenal glands
  • New renal arteries are picked up during ascent while the inferior vessels regress; if they persist they are supernumerary (accessory) vessels, which are end arteries
Fetal urine and amniotic fluid
  • The placenta clears fetal waste, but once functional the fetal kidneys produce amniotic fluid for the rest of pregnancy
  • Swallowing amniotic fluid aids development of the kidneys, lungs and gut
  • Oligohydramnios: insufficient amniotic fluid, so the uterine wall constricts the fetus and causes IUGR

Bladder (weeks 4-7)
  • Cloaca divided by the urorectal septum at week 5 into the urogenital sinus (anterior) and anorectal canal (posterior)
  • Bladder enlarges between weeks 4-6. The trigone forms as the caudal mesonephric ducts are incorporated into the posterior bladder wall; the ureters then open separately into the bladder
  • Ascent of the kidneys pulls the ureters superolaterally so they enter the bladder obliquely, making the orifices valve-like against reflux
  • Anal and urogenital membranes rupture at week 7, opening to the exterior

lectures.name: Functional Anatomy of the Kidney
lectures.title: Functional Anatomy of the Kidney
lectures.framing: The kidney does five jobs (ion regulation, osmoregulation, waste removal, hormone production, gluconeogenesis), and all of them run through the nephron: filter at the glomerulus, then reabsorb or secrete along the tubule. The page follows blood and filtrate through the kidney, then the filtration barrier, the juxtaglomerular apparatus and RAAS, and finally what happens when the kidney fails (uremia and CKD bone-mineral disease).
lectures.keypoints: Kidneys get 20-25% of cardiac output, mostly to the cortex, so the medulla is ischemia-prone (acute tubular necrosis). Glomeruli in the cortex, tubules in the medulla. Protein stays out of urine by a size barrier and a charge barrier (negative GBM); nephrin in the podocyte filtration slits, mutated → congenital nephrotic syndrome. JGA = macula densa (senses tubular NaCl) + granular cells (renin) + extraglomerular mesangial cells. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to hold glomerular pressure. CKD: EPO deficiency anemia, and failed vitamin D activation → ↓ Ca, ↑ PO4 → secondary hyperparathyroidism, treated by low-phosphate diet and calcium carbonate with meals, then calcitriol, then parathyroidectomy.

blocks.html:
Kidney functions
  1. Ion regulation: balancing salt (Na+, K+) in blood and body fluids
  2. Osmoregulation: maintaining total body water
  3. Waste management: removing toxic wastes (urea, H+ to maintain blood pH)
  4. Hormone production: e.g. active vitamin D (and EPO, renin)
  5. Gluconeogenesis: makes glucose for the brain in starvation

blocks.alt: Coronal section of a kidney showing outer cortex, medullary pyramids, calyces and renal pelvis draining into the ureter
blocks.cap: The capsule covers the outer cortex (most glomeruli), while the medullary pyramids (most tubules) drain via calyces into the renal pelvis and ureter.

blocks.html:
Gross organisation
  • Capsule: surrounds the kidney; contains nerve endings
  • Cortex: outer part; most glomeruli
  • Medulla: inner part; most tubules
  • ~1 million nephrons per kidney; the nephron is the functional unit, lined by tubular epithelial cells
Renal blood flow
  • Kidneys receive 20-25% of cardiac output despite their size (heavy metabolic role); most goes to the cortex
  • The medulla gets relatively little flow, so its tubules are vulnerable in hypotension (acute tubular necrosis)
  • Path: renal artery → interlobar artery → arcuate artery → interlobular artery → afferent arteriole → glomerular capillaries → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries / vasa recta → venules → interlobar vein → renal vein
  • The efferent arteriole is kept slightly constricted by angiotensin II to maintain glomerular pressure
Filtrate path
  • Bowman's space → proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) → loop of Henle → macula densa → distal convoluted tubule (DCT) → collecting duct → renal pelvis → ureter
  • Filtrate is made by hydrostatic pressure across glomerular capillaries; filtered substances are then reabsorbed into blood or secreted into the tubule all along the nephron
  • The PCT is rich in transporters (thick brush border); the vasa recta and peritubular capillaries surround the tubules and are where substances move to and from the lumen
  • These processes are regulated by the endocrine and nervous systems

blocks.alt: Nephron with afferent arteriole, glomerular capsule, proximal and distal convoluted tubules, loop of the nephron, collecting duct and the peritubular capillary network, with the cortex-medulla junction marked
blocks.cap: Blood leaves the glomerulus by the efferent arteriole into the peritubular capillaries wrapped around the tubule, which dips from the cortex into the medulla before the collecting duct drains to the renal pelvis.

blocks.html:
Urine formation and the filtration barrier
  • Starts with ultrafiltration of plasma across the glomerular capillaries: passive movement of protein-free fluid into Bowman's space
  • Normal urine has little or no protein because of a size barrier (proteins too large) and a charge barrier (proteins and the glomerular basement membrane are both negatively charged)
  • Renal corpuscle = glomerular capillaries (endothelial and epithelial cells) + Bowman's capsule
  • Mesangial cells: with their extracellular matrix, maintain the shape of the glomerulus
  • Podocytes: finger-like foot processes that completely encircle the capillaries; the gaps between them are filtration slits (size and charge barrier)
  • Nephrin: protein in the filtration slits; mutation → loss of the barrier → massive proteinuria (congenital nephrotic syndrome, progressing to end-stage renal disease)

rows: Cells lining the thick ascending limb where it touches its own glomerulus
Senses the ionic (NaCl) content of tubular fluid as filtrate is formed, and so influences renin release

blocks.title: Clinical correlation: volume depletion
blocks.html: In volume depletion (e.g. after a marathon) afferent arteriole perfusion pressure falls, granular cells release renin, and RAAS (renin → angiotensin I → II → aldosterone) promotes Na+ reabsorption and restores intravascular volume.

blocks.alt: RAAS diagram: decreased renal perfusion releases renin, converting liver angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, then lung ACE makes angiotensin II, which drives sympathetic activity, tubular NaCl reabsorption, aldosterone secretion, arteriolar vasoconstriction and ADH release
blocks.cap: Angiotensin II acts on several targets at once (sympathetics, tubule, adrenal cortex, arterioles, posterior pituitary) to retain salt and water, and the restored perfusion feeds back to switch renin off.

blocks.html:
Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)
  1. ↓ Renal perfusion pressure (GFR) or ECF contraction → renin released from the kidney, converting liver angiotensinogen → angiotensin I
  2. ACE (pulmonary endothelium) converts angiotensin I → angiotensin II
  3. Angiotensin II causes salt and water retention, which in turn switches RAAS off:
    • ↑ Sympathetic activity (↑ HR and CO) and arteriolar vasoconstriction → ↑ BP
    • Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex → tubular Na+ Cl- reabsorption, K+ excretion, water retention (angiotensin II also does this directly)
    • Posterior pituitary ADH → thirst and collecting duct water reabsorption

rows: HTN, CHF, LVH, arrhythmias, CAD, vascular disease
Anorexia, N/V, uremic fetor, stomatitis, gastritis (→ PUD), altered mucosal barriers
EPO deficiency; Fe, folate and B12 deficiency; hyperparathyroidism causing marrow fibrosis and osteitis fibrosa cystica
Impaired humoral and cellular immunity, lymphopenia, hypocomplementemia

Neuro (apathy, fatigue, confusion, neuropathy); endocrine (glucose intolerance, dyslipidemia, infertility, ↑ catabolism); metabolic acidosis; skin (pallor, pruritus, ecchymoses, dry skin, uremic frost)
blocks.lead: Uremic syndrome: CKD-related buildup of urea, creatinine and uric acid

blocks.html:
Calcium metabolism in CKD
  • Kidneys activate vitamin D (calcidiol → calcitriol), which ↑ intestinal Ca2+ absorption and ↓ Ca2+ excretion
  • In CKD this fails → hypocalcemia with hyperphosphatemia
  • Hyperphosphatemia stimulates parathyroid hyperplasia → secondary hyperparathyroidism → bone resorption (osteitis fibrosa cystica, marrow fibrosis)
Preventing CKD hyperparathyroidism (stepwise)
  1. Control Ca and PO4: low-phosphate diet plus calcium carbonate (TUMS) with meals to bind dietary phosphate
  2. If not enough: calcitriol (negative feedback on the parathyroids reduces hyperplasia)
  3. Last line: parathyroidectomy

lectures.name: GFR Physiology
lectures.title: GFR Physiology

blocks.html:
Renal flow numbers
  • Renal blood flow (RBF): at rest ~20% of cardiac output perfuses the kidneys
  • Renal plasma flow (RPF) = (1 − hematocrit) × RBF
  • ~20% of RPF is filtered = GFR; GFR / RPF = filtration fraction
  • Worked example: CO 5 L/min, Hct 40% → RPF = (1 − 0.4) × (0.2 × 5 L/min) = 600 mL/min → GFR = 0.2 × 600 = 120 mL/min, usually normalized to a body surface area of 1.73 m2
Glomerular filtrate
  • Finely filtered extract (ultrafiltrate) of plasma: same electrolytes and solutes, but no protein or blood cells; its composition changes along the tubule
  • Filtration = Kf × (ΔP − Δπ), where Kf is the filtration coefficient and ΔP − Δπ are the Starling forces (hydrostatic minus colloid oncotic pressure differences)
  • Size: the filtrate/plasma concentration ratio falls as molecular size rises. Small molecules (e.g. insulin, 5000 MW) filter freely; Hb (68k) and albumin (69k) cannot leak through
  • Charge: the glomerular basement membrane is negative, so negatively charged particles are filtered less than positive ones of the same size

rows: Pulls fluid out toward oncotically active proteins
Holds fluid in or draws it back

blocks.alt: Glomerular capillary next to Bowman's capsule labelled Pc 47 mmHg, capillary oncotic pressure 25 mmHg, Bowman's capsule hydrostatic pressure 10 mmHg and Bowman's oncotic pressure 0 mmHg
blocks.cap: At the glomerulus capillary hydrostatic pressure (47 mmHg) outweighs capillary oncotic (25) plus Bowman's hydrostatic pressure (10), leaving a net outward pressure of about 12 mmHg, so filtration occurs.

blocks.html:
GFR autoregulation
  • GFR is closely tied to glomerular hydrostatic pressure, and so to BP
  • Held roughly constant across arterial BP of 80-170 mmHg by feedback loops, myogenic stretch responses and neurohormonal influences on renal blood flow
  • At the extremes (especially low BP) RBF and GFR change with pressure
  • Autoregulation depends on the balance of afferent vs efferent arteriole constriction and dilation

Juxtaglomerular apparatus and tubuloglomerular feedback
  • ↓ GFR → renin release from afferent arteriole granular cells → RAAS → angiotensin II and aldosterone → GFR restored
  • ↑ GFR → more Na and Cl reach the macula densa (sensed via its Na-K-2Cl transporter) → afferent arteriole vasoconstriction → GFR falls back
  • This reflex is tubuloglomerular feedback; it is impaired by diuretics (loop diuretics block the sensing transporter)

blocks.title: Triple whammy
blocks.html: A patient with CHF on an NSAID and an ACE inhibitor develops ↓ urine output, edema and rising creatinine. Low perfusion from CHF needs both prostaglandin afferent dilation and angiotensin II efferent constriction to hold GFR; blocking both causes a severe fall in GFR. Adding a diuretic (↓ volume) completes the triple whammy and the AKI risk.

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Filtration = Kf (ΔP − Δπ); obstruction ↑ Bowman's space pressure → ↓ GFR
  • RPF = (1 − Hct) × RBF; filtration fraction ~20% of RPF
  • GFR set by arteriole diameter: Ang II constricts efferent (holds GFR), prostaglandins dilate afferent
  • CHF + NSAID + ACEi → afferent constriction + efferent dilation → ↓↓ GFR
  • JGA: macula densa (TAL, senses tubular ionic content) + granular cells of afferent arteriole (store renin) + extraglomerular mesangial cells

lectures.framing: GFR is the volume of plasma filtered from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule per unit time, and it is set by Starling forces across the glomerulus, which the kidney tunes by constricting or dilating the afferent and efferent arterioles. The page builds from blood flow numbers to the filtration equation, then autoregulation, the arteriole table and tubuloglomerular feedback.
lectures.keypoints: Filtration = Kf × (ΔP − Δπ); glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure dominates, so filtration occurs. RPF = (1 − Hct) × RBF; filtration fraction ~20% → GFR ~120 mL/min. Negatively charged and large molecules (albumin, Hb) are held back. GFR is autoregulated over MAP 80-170 mmHg. ↑ GFR: dilate afferent (prostaglandins) or constrict efferent (angiotensin II); ↓ GFR: constrict afferent (NE, endothelin, NSAIDs) or dilate efferent (ACEi/ARB). Tubuloglomerular feedback: macula densa senses ↑ NaCl → afferent constriction → ↓ GFR (blunted by loop diuretics). NSAID + ACEi (+ diuretic) = triple whammy AKI.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Retroperitoneum and Posterior Abdominal Wall
lectures.framing: Retroperitoneal structures lie behind the peritoneum on the posterior abdominal wall. The page works through that wall in layers: the diaphragm and its openings, the posterior wall muscles, the lumbar plexus, then the aorta, the IVC and lymphatics, with the clinical signs each structure explains.
lectures.keypoints: Diaphragm openings: IVC at T8, esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, aorta, azygos and thoracic duct at T12 (I ate 10 eggs at 12). Central diaphragm pain is referred to the shoulder (phrenic C3-C5); peripheral is felt at the flank (intercostals). The genitofemoral nerve pierces psoas and its genital branch carries the cremaster reflex. Abdominal aorta enters at T12 and bifurcates at L4; AAA is most often between the renal and common iliac arteries (pulsatile mass, ~90% mortality if ruptured). The IVC begins at L5; the left gonadal and left suprarenal veins drain into the left renal vein. A positive psoas sign suggests appendicitis.

rows: Proximal duodenum, pancreas, ascending colon, descending colon, rectum
5 lumbar vertebrae, diaphragm, posterior wall muscles and nerves, kidneys, adrenal glands, abdominal aorta, IVC

blocks.html:
Diaphragm
  • Principal muscle of inspiration; also ↑ intra-abdominal pressure. Posteriorly attaches as low as L3-L4
  • Lateral arcuate ligament arches over quadratus lumborum; medial arcuate ligament arches over psoas major
  • Crura attach it to the vertebral bodies and meet anteriorly as the median arcuate ligament, behind which is the aortic hiatus
    • Right crus (longer, L3/L4): splits around the esophagus to form the esophageal hiatus, contributing to the lower esophageal sphincter; part forms the ligament of Treitz
    • Left crus (shorter, L2/L3)
  • Muscle fibres converge on the central tendon, which contains the vena caval foramen

Descending aorta, thoracic duct, azygos system

blocks.html:
Diaphragm: clinical, vessels and nerves
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: abdominal contents herniate through a posterolateral defect (~1 in 2200 newborns)
  • Hiatal hernia: protrusion through a weakened diaphragm, usually a widened esophageal hiatus
  • Arteries: pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic), superior and inferior phrenic (from the aorta). Veins accompany them and drain into the IVC, except the left inferior phrenic vein → left suprarenal vein
  • Motor: phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
  • Sensory: central diaphragm via the phrenic nerve, so pain is referred to the neck and shoulder; peripheral diaphragm via intercostal (T5-T11) and subcostal (T12) nerves, so pain is localized to the flank

blocks.html:
Abdominal aorta
  • Enters through the aortic hiatus at T12; bifurcates into the common iliac arteries at L4
  • Unpaired visceral branches: celiac trunk, SMA, IMA
  • Paired branches: inferior phrenic (gives the superior suprarenal arteries), middle suprarenal, renal (give the inferior suprarenal arteries), gonadal (testicular or ovarian), lumbar arteries (continuation of the posterior intercostals)
  • Median sacral artery: unpaired, continues past the bifurcation (vestigial tail artery)

blocks.title: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
blocks.html: The abdominal aorta is the most common site of aneurysm, usually between the renal and common iliac arteries, from congenital or acquired wall weakness. Usually asymptomatic until it expands or ruptures; rupture causes massive internal bleeding with ~90% mortality. A pulsatile mass may be palpable.

IVC and tributaries
  • Formed by the union of the common iliac veins at ~L5, ascends on the right, and leaves through the caval opening at ~T8
  • Tributaries: lumbar veins, renal veins, inferior phrenic veins, hepatic veins (all gut blood via the liver), right gonadal vein
  • Right gonadal vein → IVC directly; left gonadal vein → left renal vein
  • The left renal vein is longer and crosses in front of the aorta; the left suprarenal vein (with left inferior phrenic branches) drains into it
Collateral routes if the IVC is blocked
  • Ascending lumbar vein → azygos system → SVC
  • Inferior epigastric → superior epigastric vein → SVC
  • Thoracoepigastric → axillary vein → SVC: most superficial route, can produce caput medusae
Lymphatic drainage
  • GI viscera → preaortic nodes (celiac, superior and inferior mesenteric)
  • Pelvis and lower limb → common iliac nodes
  • Posterior abdominal wall and its viscera → lumbar nodes
  • All converge on the cisterna chyli (L1-L2), which gives rise to the thoracic duct

lectures.name: Reabsorption and Secretion
lectures.title: Reabsorption and Secretion: A Trip Down the Tubule

blocks.html:
Setting up the gradient
  • Apical membrane: faces the lumen; holds the transporters for solute reabsorption
  • Basolateral membrane: holds the Na/K ATPase, which keeps intracellular Na+ low and K+ high. This Na+ gradient drives Na+ reabsorption from the filtrate along the whole tubule
  • Cell polarity keeps transport unidirectional (lumen → interstitium → blood)
  • Fenestrations make glomerular capillaries ~5000× more permeable than brain capillaries
  • 150-180 L of ultrafiltrate a day; >99% of filtered Na+ salts and water reabsorbed while toxins are removed
  • Reabsorption moves water and solute from filtrate to blood; secretion moves wastes from blood into filtrate. Both are shaped by diffusion, osmotic gradients and regulators (ADH, RAAS, natriuretic peptides, prostaglandins)

blocks.lead: How much the tubule changes the filtrate (about 1 L urine per day)

rows: 15 mm; single cell layer joined by apical tight junctions; apical microvilli (brush border)

Absorbs 50-60% of solute and water, 100% glucose and amino acids, 80-90% HCO3- (via carbonic anhydrase). Na+ moves down its gradient by cotransport (glucose, amino acids, PO4, citrate) or antiport (H+, NH4+). Water follows osmotically. Organic ions (e.g. creatinine) secreted by OAT transporters
Fanconi syndrome; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (NaHCO3 loss); SGLT2 inhibitors block Na-glucose cotransport
2-14 mm; short in cortical nephrons, long and deep in juxtamedullary nephrons (best at concentrating urine)
Descending limb: little Na/K ATPase, so impermeable to solute, highly permeable to water. Ascending limb: impermeable to water, solutes move passively
12 mm; runs to its own afferent arteriole, where macula densa cells form the JGA
Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (apical) absorbs ~30% of filtered NaCl and no water. K+ back-leak makes the lumen positive, pushing Ca2+ and Mg2+ through paracellular spaces
Loop diuretics (furosemide) and Bartter syndrome: urinary Ca loss, lose medullary gradient
Thiazide-sensitive Na-Cl cotransporter extracts more solute to make urine maximally dilute. Major site of active Ca reabsorption: Ca channel → Ca-binding protein, stimulated by vitamin D
Thiazides and Gitelman syndrome: block Na-Cl, ↑ Ca channel activity, ↓ urinary Ca (used in Ca stone formers)
20 mm; many DCTs coalesce and run from cortex to renal pelvis
Passive Na+ entry through ENaC, leaving the lumen negatively charged
Negative lumen drives K+ and H+ secretion (>90% of K+ secretion)
Depends on the negative lumen created by principal cells
Aldosterone ↑ Na+ channel activity; ANP ↓ it; ADH via V2 receptors inserts aquaporins so water moves into the hypertonic medulla
K-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene) block ENaC → ↓ K+ secretion; spironolactone blocks aldosterone, entering from the basolateral (blood) side
Interfering with principal cells (no aldosterone, K-sparing diuretics) → ↑ K+ and renal tubular acidosis

blocks.title: Clinical correlation: hyperaldosteronism
blocks.html: Conn's syndrome, adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome and licorice ingestion overdrive principal cells, causing unwanted Na+ retention and hypertension (with K+ loss).

Urine concentration and dilution
  • The kidney must produce urine from 50 to 1200 mOsm/L depending on water intake and serum osmolality
  • Deep loops, hairpin turns and countercurrent flow build a high solute concentration in the medulla
  • Countercurrent multiplication: maintains a hypertonic medulla, concentrated filtrate at the loop tip and dilute filtrate in the distal cortex
  1. Filtrate enters the PCT at roughly plasma osmolality
  2. Much Na+ is reabsorbed in the PCT; in the descending limb water leaves, so luminal concentration rises to ~1200 mOsm/L at the tip
  3. In the ascending limb solute leaves (passively, then actively in the TAL) but water cannot, so the filtrate falls to ~50 mOsm/L
  4. The collecting duct removes the last water as needed: presence or absence of ADH decides how much leaves; urea also moves out of the CD to add to medullary solute

blocks.alt: Loop diagram: water (W) leaves the descending limb, solute (S) leaves the ascending limb, and water and urea (U) leave the collecting duct, with 1200 mOsm/L at the loop tip and 50 mOsm/L at the top of the ascending limb
blocks.cap: Water leaves the descending limb and solute leaves the water-tight ascending limb, so filtrate peaks at 1200 mOsm/L at the tip and falls to 50 mOsm/L before ADH-controlled water and urea exit in the collecting duct.

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• RBF ~25% of CO; ~20% of RPF filtered
  • PCT reabsorbs 50–60% of solute + water; Na-coupled glucose/amino acids/phosphate
  • Fanconi = proximal RTA + glucosuria + phosphaturia + aminoaciduria; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors → NaHCO₃ loss
  • TAL: Na-K-2Cl (loop diuretics, Bartter); K⁺ back-leak → lumen + → paracellular Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺; loops → urinary Ca loss
  • DCT: Na-Cl (thiazides, Gitelman); major site of active Ca reabsorption; thiazides ↓ urinary Ca → Ca stones
  • CD: amiloride/triamterene block principal-cell Na channel; spironolactone = aldosterone antagonist (blood side)
  • Principal cell fails (↓ aldo, K-sparing) → ↑K⁺ + RTA; α-intercalated only → ↓K⁺ + RTA

lectures.framing: Of 150-180 L of ultrafiltrate a day, more than 99% of the salt and water is reabsorbed, and every step is powered by the basolateral Na/K ATPase keeping intracellular Na+ low. The page follows the filtrate segment by segment (PCT, loop of Henle, TAL, DCT, collecting duct), pairing each transporter with the diuretic or syndrome that targets it, then shows how the loop's countercurrent arrangement concentrates or dilutes the urine.
lectures.keypoints: PCT takes 50-60% of Na+ and water, all glucose and amino acids, most HCO3- (carbonic anhydrase); Fanconi = glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria + proximal RTA; SGLT2 inhibitors and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors act here. Descending limb: permeable to water, not solute; ascending limb: impermeable to water. TAL Na-K-2Cl (~30% NaCl, no water): K+ back-leak makes the lumen positive and drives paracellular Ca/Mg reabsorption, so loop diuretics and Bartter → urinary Ca loss. DCT Na-Cl: thiazides and Gitelman ↓ urinary Ca. Principal cells (ENaC, aldosterone ↑, ANP ↓, ADH → aquaporins via V2) make the lumen negative, which drives K+ and H+ secretion; block them (no aldosterone, K-sparing diuretics) → hyperkalemia + RTA.

lectures.name: Sodium Handling by the Kidney
lectures.title: Sodium Handling by the Kidney

rows: Disorders of serum sodium are water handling problems
Hypernatremia = too little free water; hyponatremia = too much free water
Disorders of ECF volume are sodium handling problems
Edematous disorders = too much sodium; volume contraction = too little sodium

blocks.alt: Box diagram of total body water as 60% of body weight, split into intracellular fluid (40% of weight) and ECF (20%), the ECF divided into interstitial fluid (15%) and plasma (5%)
blocks.cap: Total body water is 60% of body weight: 40% intracellular and 20% extracellular, with the ECF split 15% interstitial and 5% plasma.

blocks.html:
Fluid compartments
  • TBW ≈ 60% of body weight (about 42 L in a 70 kg adult)
  • 2/3 in the ICF (~28 L); 1/3 in the ECF
  • Within the ECF, 3/4 interstitial (~10.5 L) and 1/4 plasma (~3.5 L), plus a potential third space
  • Na+ is the main ECF cation
  • Blood volume = plasma volume + cells = plasma volume / (1 − Hct) ≈ 5 L
Why sodium (ECF volume) is tightly regulated
  • Na+ salts are >90% of osmotically active ECF solute
  • Too little ECF → volume contraction, hypotension, organ hypoperfusion
  • Too much ECF → edema, ascites, pleural effusions, HTN
  • Total body Na ≠ plasma Na concentration: measured [Na] reflects water relative to Na; total body Na is judged clinically from ECF volume

blocks.alt: Nephron outline with arrows showing the share of filtered sodium reabsorbed: 60% in the PCT, 30% in the thick ascending limb, 7% in the DCT, 2-3% in the collecting ducts and under 1% excreted
blocks.cap: Most filtered Na+ is reclaimed early (60% PCT, 30% TAL), leaving only about 7% for the DCT and 2-3% for the collecting duct, where the fine regulation happens.

rows: Cotransport with glucose, amino acids, PO4; antiport with H+
Fanconi syndrome (acidotic PCT cells → glucosuria, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria); carbonic anhydrase inhibitors → NaHCO3 loss
Passive Na+ entry; driven by aldosterone (RAAS), inhibited by ANP
blocks.lead: Sodium reabsorption along the nephron (powered by basolateral Na/K ATPase throughout)

rows: ↓ Renal perfusion pressure and renal sympathetic activity
Renin from the JGA → RAAS. Fires with true ECF contraction (Na depletion, diuretics, hemorrhage, diarrhea) and perceived contraction (CHF, cirrhosis, renal artery stenosis), where it is maladaptive
Atrial and ventricular stretch from ECF excess
Release ANP and BNP → Na and water loss, ↓ renal sympathetic activity
Alter autonomic tone and cardiac output
Main effector of ECF contraction (too little Na)

Systemic vasoconstriction (↑ BP, perfusion); ↑ Na-coupled cotransport in the PCT; ↑ aldosterone; efferent arteriole constriction holds GFR and ↑ filtration fraction, raising peritubular oncotic pressure (π) to favour reabsorption
Acts on the collecting ducts: ↑ Na/K ATPase; ↑ number and activity of Na+ channels; ↑ principal cell and α-intercalated cell activity → Na+ retention, K+ secretion, H+ excretion (alkalosis)
Mainly osmoreceptors; also angiotensin II and ↓ ECF
Vasoconstriction (including the efferent arteriole → ↑ filtration fraction → ↑ proximal Na and water reabsorption); aquaporins → water and urea reabsorption in the CD
Counter angiotensin II: dilate the afferent arteriole to preserve GFR; inhibit Na/K ATPase → natriuresis throughout the nephron
Shift fluid from vascular to interstitial space (↓ effective ECF); inhibit the CD passive Na+ channel; natriuresis

blocks.title: Aldosterone excess and prostaglandin blockade
blocks.html: Aldosterone or its mimics cause Na retention and HTN: primary aldosteronism (Conn's), congenital adrenal hyperplasia, Cushing's syndrome, true black licorice (apparent mineralocorticoid excess). NSAIDs and coxibs block prostaglandins and cause Na retention, HTN and renal failure, especially when RAAS is already high (e.g. on diuretics).

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• House's law: ECF volume disorders = Na problems; serum [Na] disorders = water problems
  • RAAS fires in true ECF contraction (hemorrhage, diuretics) and "imagined" (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrotic)
  • Aldosterone → Na retention, K⁺ secretion, alkalosis; mimics: Conn's, Cushing's, licorice
  • ANP/BNP block CD Na channel → natriuresis; NSAIDs block PGs → Na retention, HTN, renal failure

lectures.framing: Na+ salts are over 90% of ECF osmoles, so total body sodium determines ECF volume, and the kidney regulates it through volume sensors that switch on effectors (angiotensin II, aldosterone, ADH) or their counterweights (prostaglandins, ANP and BNP). The page sets up House's law and the fluid compartments, then follows Na+ reabsorption segment by segment, then the sensors and effectors.
lectures.keypoints: House's law: serum [Na] disorders are water problems; ECF volume disorders are sodium problems (edema = too much Na, volume contraction = too little). Total body Na ≠ serum [Na]. TBW = 60% of weight: 2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF; ECF is 3/4 interstitial and 1/4 plasma. Na+ reabsorption: PCT ~60% > TAL ~30% > DCT ~7% > CD 2-3%. Kidneys sense ↓ perfusion and fire RAAS in true contraction (hemorrhage, diuretics) and perceived contraction (CHF, cirrhosis, renal artery stenosis, maladaptive). Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole → ↑ filtration fraction → ↑ peritubular oncotic pressure → reabsorption. Aldosterone → Na retention, K+ secretion, alkalosis. NSAIDs remove prostaglandin natriuresis → Na retention, HTN, renal failure. ANP/BNP block the CD Na channel.

lectures.name: Edema and Volume Status
lectures.title: Edema and Volume Status

blocks.html:
Edema
  • Edema: excessive interstitial fluid volume; anasarca = widespread edema
  • "Where salt goes, water follows": edema is a sodium handling problem
  • Can be interspersed among cells (pedal or pulmonary edema) or sequestered in a potential third space (burn site, pleural effusion, ascites)
  • Forms when Starling forces favour fluid movement from the intravascular compartment → interstitium
  • Generalized edema most often reflects cardiac, liver or renal disease; localized edema reflects local trauma, venous or lymphatic obstruction
  • DDx of edema: CHF, liver cirrhosis, CKD, pulmonary HTN

rows: Right or left heart failure, pulmonary HTN, pericarditis, lymphatic obstruction, IVC or venous obstruction, incompetent valves
End-stage liver disease (↓ albumin production), nephrotic syndrome (↑ albumin loss)
blocks.lead: Starling forces and edema: UF = kUF × (ΔP − Δπ)

blocks.html:
Clinical assessment of ECF
  • ECF has two compartments, interstitial and intravascular (plus a potential third space), and the exam samples several at once
  • Bloodwork: BNP (↑ with myocardial stretch)
  • Imaging: CXR; echo; ultrasound of lungs, central veins, hepatic and portal veins
  • Invasive: central venous pressure monitoring, Swan-Ganz catheter

rows: Distressed, tachypneic, sitting upright, unable to speak full sentences: pulmonary edema. Jaundice, icterus, ascites: liver disease
Dizzy, unsteady, confused, more comfortable lying flat; dry mucous membranes, ↓ skin turgor, no edema; pallor (look for bleeding, including DRE)
HTN in renal causes; BP normal or low in heart or liver failure
Weak thready pulse, cool extremities; tachycardia (>100-120); hypotension (<90/60) or postural SBP drop >20 mmHg. Judge against background BP; in the young postural tachycardia may be the only sign
↓ Fremitus and dullness to percussion: effusion. Late inspiratory crackles or wheeze: interstitial edema
Abnormal pulses or murmur: valvular disease. Displaced apex and S3: CHF. JVP >3-4 cm: overload, or LV, pulmonary, RV or pericardial disease. Pitting edema: cardiac, liver or renal
JVP may be flat (lower the bed to see it)

blocks.title: Caveat: mixed compartments
blocks.html: A patient can be expanded in one compartment and contracted in another. In CHF the arterial (intravascular) compartment looks contracted from LV failure, driving RAAS, while the venous side is overloaded from Na retention: ↑ JVP, congested pulmonary circulation (pulmonary edema) and an expanded interstitium (pedal edema, ascites, effusions). Here there is too much salt in one compartment and too little in another, and diuretics may further contract the intravascular space and cause tissue hypoperfusion.

Remember
  • Overload of water changes osmolality and shifts fluid between ECF and ICF
  • Overload of isotonic fluid just redistributes within the ECF

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• ECF contraction: dry mucosa, ↓ turgor, tachycardia, flat JVP; postural tachycardia may be the only sign in the young → isotonic saline
  • ECF overload: edema, ascites, effusions, ↑ JVP; BP ↑ (renal) or normal/low (heart, liver) → diuretics/dialysis

lectures.framing: Edema is excess interstitial fluid, and because water follows salt it is a problem of sodium handling, not water handling. The page explains edema through the Starling forces (permeability, hydrostatic pressure, oncotic pressure), then sets out the bedside assessment of ECF overload vs ECF contraction and the caveat that one patient can be overloaded in one compartment and depleted in another.
lectures.keypoints: UF = kUF × (ΔP − Δπ): edema from ↑ permeability (histamine, kinins, substance P, sepsis), ↑ ΔP (venous obstruction, heart failure, Na retention, dihydropyridine CCBs) or ↓ Δπ (liver failure, nephrotic syndrome). Generalized edema = heart, liver or kidney; localized = trauma, venous or lymphatic obstruction. Overload: JVP >3-4 cm, S3 and displaced apex, crackles, effusion, pitting edema; BP ↑ in renal causes, normal or low in heart or liver failure. Contraction: tachycardia, hypotension, postural SBP drop >20, flat JVP, dry mucosa; in the young postural tachycardia may be the only sign. Treat contraction with isotonic fluid, overload by removing salt (diuretics, dialysis). Excess water shifts between ECF and ICF; excess isotonic fluid stays in the ECF.

lectures.name: Water Handling by the Kidney
lectures.title: Water Handling by the Kidney

blocks.html:
Why water handling matters
  • Intracellular fluid volume is needed for cell function
  • Cell swelling (↑ ICF) is dangerous where tissue has little room to expand (brain inside the skull); rapid changes in cell size can cause permanent dysfunction
  • ~180 L filtered a day vs ~1 L urine, so most water is reabsorbed
  • Water handling is independent of the kidney's other functions: the same solute or waste can be excreted in very different volumes, so urine solute concentrations must be read against urine concentration
ADH (vasopressin)
  • Released from the posterior pituitary when hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense ↑ osmolality, or with ECF volume contraction; ↑ osmolality also triggers thirst
  • ↓ Osmolality switches ADH off, protecting swelling-sensitive brain cells
  • Actions:
    • Via V2 receptors, inserts aquaporins into the apical and basolateral membranes of collecting duct (principal) cells
    • ↑ TAL cotransporter activity and ↑ urea reabsorption, which strengthen countercurrent multiplication and the salty medulla

rows: ↓ Effective circulating volume; ADH rises exponentially in extreme volume depletion, so ECF takes over regulation
Pain, emotion, stress; endocrine disorders (thyroid disease, adrenal insufficiency); CNS or lung tumours or infections
SSRIs, ecstasy (MDMA), desmopressin (ddAVP), oxytocin, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, phenothiazines, chlorpropamide, clofibrate
blocks.lead: What releases ADH (non-osmotic stimuli can override osmolality and retain water even as cells swell)

rows: Active NaCl transport in the TAL (salty medulla); thin descending limb permeable to water; thin ascending limb impermeable to water but permeable to solute
Adequate urine production via adequate GFR; passive and active NaCl removal in the TAL and DCT
Water reabsorption in the cortical CD in response to ADH; water and urea reabsorption in the medullary CD in response to ADH
blocks.lead: Requirements for concentrating vs diluting urine (identical until the collecting duct, where ADH decides)

blocks.html:
Serum sodium and osmolality
  • House's law 1: disorders of serum sodium are water handling problems (hypernatremia = too little free water; hyponatremia = too much)
  • Measured serum Na is the concentration of Na in the ECF, showing how much water is present relative to Na. It does not show total body Na (a clinical assessment of ECF volume)
  • Na is the main ECF osmole, so serum Na is a cheap, usually reliable estimate of osmolality: serum osmolality = 2 × Na + urea + glucose
  • True osmolality high → water moves ICF → ECF and cells shrink; low → ECF → ICF and cells swell

rows: Na >144 mmol/L: less water in the ECF relative to Na
Na <136 mmol/L: more water in the ECF relative to Na
Loss of water (renal or non-renal), not a gain of Na
Unusual in outpatients because thirst is so strong, even if ADH is missing (central DI) or ineffective (nephrogenic DI). If present, suspect a CNS problem with an ADH disorder or no access to water
Usually means low osmolality, but pseudohyponatremia has normal or high osmolality (hyperlipidemia, uncontrolled diabetes or mannitol, very high immunoglobulins in myeloma)
Acute: brain cells shrink. Chronic: brain cells accumulate other osmolytes to defend volume, so correct slowly
Often coexists with ECF disorders (hypovolemia, ↓ effective circulating volume in CHF and cirrhosis), which trigger thirst, RAAS and ADH and so drive hyponatremia

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• ADH released mainly for ↑ osmolality; ECF contraction is weaker but ultimately potent
  • ADH → V2 → aquaporins in principal cells; also ↑ urea reabsorption in medullary CD
  • Non-osmotic ADH: ↓ effective volume, pain/stress, SSRIs, carbamazepine, CNS/lung tumours

lectures.framing: Water handling runs largely independently of the kidney's other jobs: the same solute load can leave in a small or a large volume. The switch is ADH acting on the collecting duct, working on the medullary gradient built by countercurrent multiplication. The page covers why cell volume matters, ADH (stimuli and actions), what concentrated vs dilute urine requires, and then the dysnatremias, which are disorders of water rather than sodium.
lectures.keypoints: Serum [Na] disorders are water problems (House's law 1). Serum osmolality = 2 × Na + urea + glucose. ADH (posterior pituitary) responds mainly to ↑ osmolality; extreme volume depletion drives ADH exponentially and overrides osmolality. Non-osmotic triggers: ↓ effective circulating volume, pain, stress, CNS or lung tumours or infection, SSRIs, ecstasy, desmopressin. ADH → V2 → aquaporins in collecting duct cells, plus ↑ TAL transport and urea reabsorption. Dilute urine needs adequate GFR, NaCl removal in TAL and DCT, and no ADH. Hypernatremia (>144) = water loss, rare when thirst works, so suspect a CNS or ADH problem; correct chronic cases slowly. Hyponatremia (<136) = failure to excrete free water; normal or high osmolality = pseudohyponatremia.

lectures.name: Hyponatremia and Hypernatremia
lectures.title: Hyponatremia and Hypernatremia

blocks.alt: sodium disorders overview.svg

blocks.html:
Hypernatremia
  • Serum Na >144 mmol/L: water moves out of cells, so cells shrink
  • Almost always a lack of free water; rarely Na gain (seawater, iatrogenic IV fluids, mineralocorticoid excess)
  • Unusual if the patient has an intact thirst reflex, access to water and the ability to drink (seen at extremes of age)
  • Symptoms: altered mental status, twitching, seizures, coma; ruptured cerebral vessels in severe cases

rows: Brain injury: trauma (basal skull fracture), neurosurgery (esp. pituitary), space-occupying lesions (tumours, sarcoidosis), infection (meningitis, encephalitis), hypoxic brain damage, idiopathic

Congenital; drugs impairing ADH action (lithium, V2 inhibitors "-vaptans"); chronic electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypercalcemia); impaired concentrating ability (CKD, loop diuretics, tubulointerstitial disease: amyloid, sickle cell, obstruction)
Yes, if water intake cannot keep up
Yes, if water intake cannot keep up

blocks.alt: Flowchart: clinical assessment of hypernatremia by ECF volume, urine volume, urine osmolality and ddAVP response
blocks.cap: Hypernatremia algorithm: ECF expanded (rare) means Na gain; low urine volume means non-renal losses (GI, skin, respiratory, osmotic laxatives); high urine volume with low urine Osm is DI, split by ddAVP response; high urine Osm points to diuretics or osmotic diuresis (glucose, mannitol).

blocks.html:
Reading the hypernatremia workup
  • Total body Na is judged clinically from ECF volume (flat JVP, dry membranes, ↓ skin turgor = low)
  • Volume-contracted patients avidly reabsorb Na, so urine Na is low
  • FENa = (NaU/NaP) / (CrU/CrP) × 100 ("SU/P over CU/P"; put Cr in the same units). Normally ~99% of filtered Na is reabsorbed, so FENa <1%; very low values mean severe volume contraction
  • High urine Osm with high urine Na+K: urine osmoles may be electrolytes, urea or glucose (hypernatremia + diabetes mellitus = high urine Osm from glucose)

Treating hypernatremia
  1. Identify and correct the underlying cause
  2. Calculate the free water deficit:
    • TBWcurrent × [Na]current = TBWdesired × [Na]desired
    • Free water deficit = TBWdesired − TBWcurrent = TBWcurrent × ([Na]current/140 − 1)
    • Estimate TBW as 50% of body weight in water deficit (not the usual 60%); use 140 mmol/L as desired [Na]
    • Add ongoing free water losses (urine, GI, insensible) of ~800-1000 mL/day
  3. Give oral (or NG) water where possible, otherwise D5W or IV hypotonic fluids (never plain water IV: it lyses cells). D5W is limited to ~300-350 mL/h or hyperglycemia and osmotic diuresis follow
  4. Correct slowly, <10 mmol/L per 24 h: brain cells have recruited osmolytes, so fast correction causes cerebral edema

Hyponatremia
  • Serum Na <136 mmol/L: too much water relative to Na; risk is brain swelling
  • Symptoms depend on timing; if acute: headache, nausea, vomiting, restlessness, disorientation, seizures
  • Confirm it is "true": plasma Osm must also be low
  • Pseudohyponatremia (plasma Osm high or normal): hyperglycemia or mannitol pull water out of cells and dilute Na, but cells shrink rather than swell. Correct Na up by 1 mmol/L per 3-4 mmol/L glucose above normal (Na 125 with glucose 35 → "true" Na ~135). Older lab methods also gave false values with dyslipidemia
  • True hyponatremia = inadequate free water excretion, most often from inappropriately elevated ADH (SIADH or non-osmotic ADH stimuli)
  • Ask why the kidney is not making dilute urine; the 3 requirements are adequate GFR/urine flow, tubules extracting solute, and absence of ADH

blocks.alt: Flowchart: clinical assessment of hyponatremia by plasma osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, GFR and ECF volume
blocks.cap: Hyponatremia algorithm: confirm low plasma Osm, then urine Osm <100 means excess water intake; otherwise urine Na <20 (RAAS on: CHF, cirrhosis, nephrosis or non-renal losses) vs >20, where normal GFR with normal ECF is where SIADH lives.

rows: ADH appropriately off: excess water ingestion or iatrogenic
RAAS activated: ECF expanded with ↓ effective volume (CHF, cirrhosis, nephrosis) or ECF contracted with non-renal losses (GI, third space)

blocks.html:
Treating hyponatremia
  • Restrict all sources of water (oral, NG feeds, hypotonic IV) and correct the cause of ADH release where possible (stop drugs, restore ECF, treat CHF)
  • Symptomatic: correct rapidly with saline hypertonic to the urine (e.g. 3% NaCl, ~513 mmol/L Na). Most seizures stop within 3-7 mmol/L of correction; once symptoms improve, slow to a max of 8-10 mmol/L/day
  • Asymptomatic: fluid restrict and correct slowly
  • True SIADH (rare) may need a vaptan (induces nephrogenic DI) or oral urea

blocks.title: Osmotic demyelination
blocks.html: Correcting hyponatremia too fast shrinks adapted brain cells and causes osmotic demyelination. Keep correction to 8-10 mmol/L/day once symptoms settle.

blocks.title: Why 0.9% saline worsens SIADH
blocks.html: Compare what goes in with what comes out. With SIADH (plasma Osm 270, urine Osm 600), 1 L of NS delivers ~300 mOsm. The euvolemic patient excretes that solute in a concentrated urine: 300 ÷ 600 = 0.5 L. Net result is a gain of 0.5 L free water, so Na falls further. Use fluid hypertonic to the urine (3% saline, ~1000 mOsm/L).

rows: Dementia, dry mucous membranes, flat JVP, no edema
Dementia, mild HTN, diabetes, on an SSRI, normal exam
Serum Na 160, Cr 90 µmol/L; urine Na 15, Cr 6.0 mmol/L, Osm 600
Serum Na 115, Cr 60, K 5, glucose 5, Osm 245; urine Osm 383, Na 80, K 80
High serum Na + low urine Na = ECF depletion (holding on to Na). FENa = (15/160)/(6000/90) × 100 = 0.14% = severe volume contraction; high urine Osm = very high ADH state
Normal glucose and low serum Osm = true hyponatremia. Concentrated urine with high urine Na in a euvolemic patient; confirm renal, adrenal and thyroid axes are intact → SIADH, likely from the SSRI
BW 50 kg → TBW 25 L. Deficit = 25 × (160/140 − 1) = 3.6 L. 20 mmol/L to correct at ≤10/day → over 2 days: D5W 1.8 L/24 h (75 mL/h) for 48 h, plus ongoing losses
Remove the cause (rule out brain infection/tumour), restrict free water, correct slowly (≤8-10 mmol/L/day) as she is asymptomatic. If symptomatic: 3% NaCl, hypertonic to urine

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Hypernatremia (Na >144) = water deficit; correct ≤10 mmol/L per day (cerebral edema); oral water or D5W
  • Hyponatremia (Na <136): check Posm; normal/high = pseudohyponatremia (glucose, mannitol)
  • Symptomatic → 3% saline first; asymptomatic → fluid restrict, ≤8–10 mmol/L/day
  • SIADH: 0.9% saline can lower Na further (hypotonic to a concentrated urine)

lectures.framing: Sodium disorders are water disorders: plasma [Na] reports how much water there is relative to sodium, while total body sodium is judged by ECF volume. Hypernatremia (Na >144) is almost always a lack of free water, and hyponatremia (Na <136) is almost always excess free water with ADH on. The page runs hypernatremia (DI, algorithm, free water deficit), then hyponatremia (pseudo vs true, algorithm, correction), then two worked cases.
lectures.keypoints: DI: urine Osm rises with ddAVP = central DI, no change = nephrogenic DI (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia); dipsogenic DI does not cause hypernatremia. Free water deficit = TBWcurrent × ([Na]current/140 − 1), with TBW = 50% body weight, then add ~800-1000 mL/day ongoing losses. Correct hypernatremia <10 mmol/L per 24 h (cerebral edema). In hyponatremia first confirm plasma Osm is truly low (glucose: add 1 mmol/L Na per 3-4 mmol/L glucose above normal). SIADH = low plasma Osm, high urine Osm, urine Na >20, normal GFR, euvolemic. Symptomatic → 3% saline (hypertonic to the urine), then max 8-10 mmol/L/day to avoid osmotic demyelination; 0.9% saline can worsen SIADH.

lectures.name: Acid Base Disturbances
lectures.title: Acid Base Disturbances

blocks.alt: acid base overview.svg

blocks.html:
Basics
  • Normal pH 7.35-7.45; outside 6.8-7.8 causes permanent cell damage and death
  • Normal values: pH 7.40 (7.38-7.42), pCO2 40 (38-42), HCO3 24 (22-26)
  • Daily load: ~15,000 mmol CO2 (lungs) and ~1 mmol/kg nonvolatile acid, mostly sulfuric acid (kidneys)
  • ABG gives pH, pCO2 and HCO3 (tCO2 is interchangeable with HCO3)
  • Acidosis: process lowering pH (↑ pCO2 and/or ↓ HCO3). Alkalosis: process raising pH (↓ pCO2 and/or ↑ HCO3)

Anion gap
  • AG = Na − Cl − HCO3 (predominant cation minus the two predominant anions); normal ~12, made up mostly of negatively charged proteins
  • Expected AG falls by 3 for every 10 g/L albumin below normal (~40 g/L)
  • ΔAG = observed AG − expected AG; normally ~0
  • Example: Na 140, Cl 120, HCO3 10, albumin 30 → expected AG = 12 − 3 = 9; observed = 140 − 120 − 10 = 10; ΔAG = 1, so the AG is not significantly ↑
  • AG acidosis: H+ accumulates with an unmeasured anion; HCO3 falls buffering it while Cl is unchanged, so the AG widens
  • Non-AG acidosis: H+ accumulates without another anion; Cl rises as much as HCO3 falls (hyperchloremic)

blocks.alt: Gamblegram bars comparing normal anion gap, anion gap metabolic acidosis and non anion gap metabolic acidosis
blocks.cap: In AGMA the fall in HCO<sub>3</sub> is matched by a bigger anion gap; in NAGMA it is matched by a rise in chloride, so the gap stays normal.

blocks.html:
Renal acid handling
  • Proximal tubule reabsorbs filtered HCO3 via carbonic anhydrase; in acidosis it ↑ HCO3 reabsorption and ↑ NH4+ (ammonia) secretion, which traps H+ secreted downstream
  • Distal tubule secretes H+ through the α-intercalated cell, driven by aldosterone; excreted acid appears in urine as ammonium (NH4+)
  • Principal cell Na+ reabsorption leaves a negative charge in the lumen, which pulls K+ or H+ into the urine

blocks.html:
Reading the pattern
  • pH and pCO2 moving in the same direction = metabolic; opposite = respiratory
  • In a primary metabolic disorder HCO3 changes first and pCO2 compensates; in a primary respiratory disorder pCO2 changes first
  • Compensation short of the expected ratio means a second primary disorder. Examples: metabolic acidosis on metabolic alkalosis can give a near-normal pH and HCO3 but a ↑ AG; salicylate overdose gives metabolic acidosis plus a respiratory alkalosis larger than compensation

blocks.html:
Urine anion gap (urine net charge)
  • Compare urine cations (Na + K) with urine anion (Cl). If Cl ≫ Na + K, another cation must be present, and that is NH4+ (not measured directly)
  • Lots of NH4+ and urine pH <5.5 = distal nephron is maximally acidifying → the cause is GI or proximal HCO3 loss
  • Cl ≤ Na + K = little NH4+ → distal tubule acidification problem (type I or IV RTA)
  • Pitfall: a large load of other urine anions can make NH4+ look inadequate

Treating metabolic acidosis
  1. Treat the underlying cause: methanol or ethylene glycol → fomepizole or ethanol to compete for alcohol dehydrogenase (often plus hemodialysis); aspirin overdose may need hemodialysis; DKA needs insulin
  2. Avoid giving buffer (NaHCO3): it generates CO2 and worsens intracellular acidosis (especially with breathing problems), and its Na+ goes straight to the ECF (risky with volume overload or poor cardiac function)
  3. NaHCO3 is indicated when pH <7.10 or HCO3 <10-12 mmol/L: small further changes then drop pH rapidly

blocks.html:
Metabolic alkalosis: diagnosis and treatment
  • High urine K+ or TTKG confirms aldosterone is present and working
  • Usually accompanied by hypokalemia (mineralocorticoid action on the principal cell)
  • Ongoing low K+ tricks the kidney into acting as if acidotic, perpetuating renal acid secretion, so K+ must be replaced

Approach to acid-base cases
  1. Look at pH: acidosis or alkalosis. Then decide metabolic (HCO3 low in acidosis, high in alkalosis) vs respiratory (pCO2 high in acidosis, low in alkalosis)
  2. Check whether compensation is adequate and its chronicity (ratios above); inadequate = second disorder
  3. Calculate the AG and ΔAG, correcting for albumin
  4. Build the differential: AGMA → osmolal gap, toxins, lactate, ketoacids, salicylate, uremia; NAGMA → HCO3 loss (GI, PT) vs failure to excrete H+ (DT); metabolic alkalosis → ECF expanded (primary) vs contracted (secondary mineralocorticoid)

lectures.framing: pH is held at 7.35-7.45 by lungs excreting CO2 and kidneys excreting H+ (and reclaiming HCO3). The page builds the tools first (ABG, anion gap, renal acid handling and RTA), then the four primary disorders with their expected compensation, then metabolic acidosis (AGMA vs NAGMA) and metabolic alkalosis, and ends with a stepwise approach applied to four cases.
lectures.keypoints: AG = Na − Cl − HCO3, expected 12, ↓ 3 per 10 g/L albumin below 40; ΔAG = observed − expected. Compensation: metabolic acidosis 1 HCO3 : 1 pCO2, metabolic alkalosis 10 : 7, respiratory acidosis 10 pCO2 : 1 (acute) or 4 (chronic) HCO3, respiratory alkalosis 10 : 2 (acute) or 4 (chronic). AGMA = MUDPILES; check the osmolal gap (2 × Na + urea + glucose) for methanol and ethylene glycol. NAGMA = HCO3 loss (GI, proximal RTA) or failed distal H+ secretion; the urine anion gap (Cl vs Na + K) shows whether NH4+ is excreted. Type I RTA = hypokalemic (α-intercalated cell), type IV = hyperkalemic (aldosterone). Give NaHCO3 only if pH <7.10 or HCO3 <10-12. Metabolic alkalosis = too much mineralocorticoid; urine Cl <10 = secondary (volume contraction).

lectures.name: Potassium Handling by the Kidney
lectures.title: Potassium Handling by the Kidney: Hypokalemia and Hyperkalemia

blocks.html:
K+ basics
  • Normal [K]ECF 3.5-5 mmol/L; [K]ICF ~150 mmol/L, maintained by Na/K-ATPase
  • Altered membrane potential → cardiac arrhythmia and neuromuscular dysfunction, potentially fatal

rows: PR 0.16 s, QRS 0.06 s, QT 0.4 s
QRS widens, P waves flatten and PR prolongs, progressing to a sine wave → risk of VT/VF
PR widening, ST depression, U wave appears
ST depression, T wave inversion, prominent U wave

blocks.html:
Regulation of K+
  • Dietary K 40-120 mmol/day; 90-95% must be excreted by the kidneys (GI excretion ↑ in advanced kidney disease)
  • Most net secretion/reabsorption happens in the principal cell of the cortical collecting duct (CCD)
  • Aldosterone (released for RAAS activation or high ECF K) drives K secretion in the CCD
  • K-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene) block the principal cell Na channel, so the lumen is less negative and less K is drawn out
  • Urine flow past the CCD maintains the K secretion gradient; low urine Na also impairs secretion
  • Alkalosis: less H+ secreted by α-intercalated cells, so more K+ is secreted
  • Immediate response to a K load is to shift K into cells via Na/K-ATPase, stimulated by insulin and catecholamines; renal excretion takes longer

Three mechanisms (disorders usually need two to fail)
  1. Intake: diet, tissue necrosis, massive hemolysis
  2. Output: mostly renal under aldosterone, some GI
  3. Shift: insulin, β-adrenergic receptors, Na/K-ATPase, rare periodic paralyses, rapid cell expansion (treated pernicious anemia)

Measuring renal K handling
  • Spot urine K is often used but is unhelpful when plasma K is near normal
  • TTKG estimates the K gradient between CCD lumen and blood, correcting for urine concentration
  • TTKG = (Kurine × Osmblood) / (Kblood × Osmurine)
  • TTKG >7: aldosterone present and working. In hyperkalemia TTKG should be >7; if not, there is an aldosterone problem
  • TTKG <2: aldosterone absent or blocked, or inadequate urine Na and flow

blocks.cap: Hypokalemia: low urine K (<15 mmol/day or TTKG <2) with acidosis = lower GI loss, with alkalosis = remote diuretics or vomiting; high urine K (TTKG >7) with acidosis = RTA or DKA, with alkalosis split by blood pressure (HTN = mineralocorticoid excess; no HTN = vomiting, Bartter's/Gitelman's, diuretics).

blocks.html:
Hypokalemia: diagnosis and treatment
  • The kidney should conserve K; spot urine K >30 or TTKG >7 = renal wasting
  • Metabolic alkalosis → mineralocorticoid excess (↑ principal and α-intercalated cell activity)
  • Metabolic acidosis → diarrhea or RTA
  • Urine Na >20 (low Cl) with ECF contraction → diuretics, vomiting, Bartter's/Gitelman's
  • Treat urgently with digitalis toxicity, during DKA therapy (insulin shifts K in) and with symptoms (arrhythmia, weakness)
  • Quick but not too quick: oral therapy lets K equilibrate between ECF and ICF and avoids overshoot; IV <40 mmol/h; several hundred mmol may be needed in total

blocks.alt: Flowchart: clinical approach to hyperkalemia by urinary K excretion
blocks.cap: Hyperkalemia: after ruling out pseudohyperkalemia, low urine K (TTKG <2) is inappropriate and implies inadequate aldosterone (drugs: ACEi, ARB, NSAIDs, K-sparing diuretics; or Addison's, type IV RTA), while high urine K (TTKG >7) is appropriate and implies shift or increased intake.

blocks.html:
Hyperkalemia: diagnosis
  • Main danger is arrhythmia: always check the ECG; a completely normal ECG suggests pseudohyperkalemia
  • Take a careful medication history and assess renal function and urine volume
  • Urine K <30 or TTKG <2 → impaired secretion, inadequate aldosterone
  • With metabolic acidosis → type IV RTA (failure of both principal and α-intercalated cells from lack or blockade of aldosterone)

Hyperkalemia: treatment in order
  1. Confirm: exclude pseudohyperkalemia, check the ECG (treat while awaiting confirmation if in doubt)
  2. Stabilize the heart: 1 ampoule 10% calcium gluconate; it does not lower K but stabilizes the myocardial membrane threshold
  3. Shift K into cells: IV insulin + glucose (prevents hypoglycemia), β-agonist (salbutamol), bicarbonate (for NAGMA)
  4. Eliminate: renal (fluids, loop diuretics, bicarbonate, mineralocorticoid such as fludrocortisone); colonic K-binding resins (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, patiromer, sodium polystyrene); dialysis if renal function cannot be restored quickly

blocks.html:
• TTKG >7 = aldosterone working; <2 = absent/blocked or poor distal Na/flow
  • HyperK⁺: ECG first; Ca gluconate protects the heart; shift (insulin-glucose, β-agonist); then eliminate
  • Normal ECG → think pseudohyperkalemia (hemolysis, very high cell counts)
  • HypoK⁺: urine K >30 or TTKG >7 = renal wasting; oral preferred, IV <40 mmol/h

lectures.framing: K+ is the main intracellular cation, and its ICF:ECF ratio sets the membrane potential, so small plasma changes threaten the heart and muscles. Plasma K reflects intake, output (mostly renal, via aldosterone at the CCD) and shift between ICF and ECF; disorders usually need two of the three to fail. The page covers regulation and the TTKG, then hypokalemia and hyperkalemia (causes, diagnosis, treatment) and five cases.
lectures.keypoints: TTKG = (Kurine × Osmblood) / (Kblood × Osmurine): >7 = aldosterone present and working, <2 = aldosterone absent/blocked or low distal Na and flow. Hypokalemia with urine K >30 or TTKG >7 = renal wasting; metabolic alkalosis points to mineralocorticoid excess, acidosis to diarrhea or RTA. Replace K orally where possible, IV <40 mmol/h. Hyperkalemia: check the ECG first (normal ECG suggests pseudohyperkalemia), then calcium gluconate to protect the heart, shift (insulin + glucose, β-agonist, bicarbonate) and eliminate (diuretics, resins, dialysis). Drugs causing hyperkalemia: ACEi, ARB, aliskiren, K-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin. Gitelman's vs thiazide: both give low urine Ca; Gitelman's wastes Mg.

blocks.title: ½ NS worked through
blocks.html: 1 L of ½ NS = 500 mL of 0.9% saline (all ECF) + 500 mL free water (333 mL ICF, 167 mL ECF). Net: 333 mL ICF, 667 mL ECF.

1. ECF volume contraction
  • Use isotonic saline or something else that stays in the ECF (blood, colloid); trials have not shown colloid beats crystalloid
  • IV vs oral depends on how fast correction is needed, the threat to circulation and the risk of overshooting
  • No formula reliably predicts the volume needed (they ignore ongoing losses in urine, sweat, feces, breath), so give a fluid challenge of isotonic crystalloid
  • Judge response clinically: BP rising? pulse falling? postural changes persisting? JVP becoming visible? urine output improving? Swan-Ganz/CVP improving? CXR becoming "wet"?
  • Hypovolemic shock (e.g. GI hemorrhage): rapid, "wide open"
  • Less severe hypovolemia or cardiac disease: go slowly to prevent pulmonary edema

2. Effects on electrolytes (water problems)
  • If the problem is water overload or underload, decide whether you want to add or remove free water
  • The effect depends on what goes in (infusate) vs what comes out (urine)
  • In Na disorders, fluid hypertonic to the urine → serum Na ↑; fluid hypotonic to the urine → serum Na ↓
  • Infused K behaves like Na in the ECF (Na/K-ATPase swaps it for Na)

3. Metabolic acidosis (e.g. diarrhea with low HCO3 and K)
  • Build a fairly isotonic hybrid: ½ NS (77 mmol/L) + one 50 mL ampoule NaHCO3 (50 mmol) + 20 mmol KCl per litre → effective Na ~147
  • KCl takes time to move from ECF into ICF, so prefer oral K, or limit IV to 10-20 mmol boluses or 40 mmol/L infusate run relatively slowly (<250 mL/h)

4. Maintenance fluids
  • Daily intake ~1.5 L water, 100-250 mmol Na, 50-100 mmol K
  • Obligate losses: ≥500 mL urine (~600 mOsm solute at a maximum 1200 mOsm/L) + 800-1000 mL insensible (stool, sweat, breath)
  • Healthy kidneys handle a range of Na and K: ½ NS with 20 mmol/L KCl gives a 70 kg patient ~200 mmol Na and ~50 mmol K per day

• NS and RL → ECF only; colloid → plasma
  • D5W = free water: 2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF; ½NS → 1/3 ICF, 2/3 ECF
  • 3% saline for symptomatic hyponatremia; D5W for hypernatremia

lectures.framing: Choosing an IV fluid means knowing which compartment it ends up in: isotonic saline stays in the ECF, free water spreads across all body water, and colloids hold fluid in the plasma. The page compares the fluids, then works through what to use and when: ECF contraction, electrolyte (water) problems, metabolic acidosis, and maintenance.
lectures.keypoints: NS (0.9%, ~154 mmol/L) stays in the ECF (plasma first, then interstitium). D5W = free water: 2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF. ½ NS = ½ isotonic saline + ½ free water: 1 L → 667 mL ECF, 333 mL ICF. Colloids stay in the plasma and draw fluid in from the interstitium. Treat ECF contraction with isotonic crystalloid as a fluid challenge judged clinically (BP, pulse, JVP, urine output, CXR); go slowly with cardiac disease. For Na disorders, fluid hypertonic to the urine raises serum Na and hypotonic fluid lowers it. Maintenance: 4-2-1 rule (70 kg → 110 mL/h); ½ NS + 20 mmol/L KCl gives ~200 mmol Na and ~50 mmol K a day.

lectures.name: Anatomy of the Pelvis
lectures.title: Anatomy of the Pelvis, Perineum and Male Reproductive Tract
lectures.framing: The pelvis houses the terminal urinary, GI and reproductive tracts and is the passage to the lower limb. The note works from bones and walls → pelvic floor and perineum → arteries, veins and nerves → male reproductive organs → their development. Two ideas organise it: the pelvic floor separates the pelvis above from the perineum below, and the testes keep the blood supply, lymph drainage and pain pathways of their posterior abdominal origin.
lectures.keypoints: The internal iliac artery supplies the pelvis; the internal pudendal artery and pudendal nerve (S2-S4) leave via the greater sciatic foramen and re-enter via the lesser sciatic foramen to supply the whole perineum. Superior gluteal vessels/nerve pass above piriformis, inferior gluteal below. Pelvic venous plexuses are valveless, so metastases (e.g. prostate) spread unpredictably. A urethral rupture collects in the superficial or deep perineal pouch depending on the level. Pain above the pelvic pain line travels with sympathetics, below it with parasympathetics; pelvic splanchnics (S2-S4) contract the detrusor. Testes drain to lumbar/preaortic nodes, scrotal skin to superficial inguinal nodes. SRY → TDF drives the male phenotype: Sertoli cells make AMH, Leydig cells make testosterone (week 8), and DHT forms the external genitalia.

blocks.html:
Bones, ligaments and walls
  • 5 bones: two hip bones (ilium, ischium and pubis fused; meet at the pubic symphysis), sacrum (sacroiliac joints) and coccyx
  • False pelvis: above the pelvic inlet, between the iliac alae; holds abdominal contents. True pelvis: below the inlet
  • Iliolumbar and posterior sacroiliac ligaments hold the sacrum to the ilium
  • Sacrospinous (sacrum → ischial spine) and sacrotuberous (sacrum → ischial tuberosity) ligaments close the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen; the lesser sciatic foramen links the perineum with the gluteal region
  • Walls: obturator internus = most of the lateral wall; piriformis = posterior wall (key landmark); pelvic floor (coccygeus + levator ani, including the puborectal sling) = inferior wall
  • Gaps in the floor: urogenital hiatus (urethra, plus vagina in females) and rectal hiatus (rectum, anal canal)
  • Pelvic organs: urethra, bladder and rectum in both sexes; plus vagina, uterus, ovaries and uterine tubes in females

blocks.lead: Perineum: everything below the pelvic floor, split by a line between the ischial tuberosities through the perineal body

blocks.html:
Perineal body and fascia
  • Perineal body: musculofibrous centre of the perineum; final support of the pelvic viscera and attachment for perineal muscles. Torn in childbirth, trauma or infection → prolapse
  • Fascial continuations from the abdominal wall: superficial fatty layer ← Camper's fascia (females); Colles' fascia ← Scarpa's fascia; deep perineal fascia ← rectus sheath

blocks.html:
Other arteries and the veins
  • Aorta bifurcates into the common iliacs at L4; these split into external iliac (lower limb) and internal iliac (pelvis) at L5/S1
  • Gonadal arteries arise directly from the aorta (testicular artery traverses the inguinal canal); superior rectal artery comes from the IMA
  • Veins follow the arteries but form plexuses (vesical, prostatic, uterine, vaginal, rectal) that drain to the internal iliac vein, except the gonadal veins (right → IVC, left → left renal vein) and the superior rectal vein (→ IMV → portal vein)
  • Pelvic plexuses are valveless: blood takes the path of least resistance, so metastases can reach any plexus unpredictably

Male reproductive organs
  • Testis: sperm form in the seminiferous tubules; covered by the tunica albuginea and the tunica vaginalis (from peritoneum)
  • Spermatic coverings: internal spermatic fascia ← transversalis fascia; cremaster ← internal oblique; external spermatic fascia ← external oblique
  • Scrotum: dartos fascia (continuous with Colles'/Scarpa's) wrinkles skin; septum divides it into two compartments
  • Testes must be 1-2 °C below body temperature: pampiniform plexus (countercurrent cooling), cremaster (pulls testes up), dartos (wrinkles skin)
  • Sperm path: epididymis (storage, maturation) → ductus deferens (in the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal; subperitoneal; ampulla) + seminal vesicle → ejaculatory duct (inside the prostate) → prostatic urethra
  • Urethra: prostatic → membranous → penile. Internal sphincter = involuntary (stops ejaculate entering bladder); external sphincter = voluntary
  • Penis: 2 corpora cavernosa (dorsal; hold 80-90% of blood in erection) and 1 corpus spongiosum (houses the penile urethra; forms the bulb and glans)

Development of the male tract
  • SRY gene → testis-determining factor (TDF); without TDF the default female phenotype develops
  • Urogenital ridge → nephrogenic cord (urinary) + gonadal ridge (genital). Primordial germ cells migrate from the yolk sac in weeks 5-6 (no migration = no gonad); gonads are indifferent until then
  • Week 7: mesonephric duct → male tract (efferent ductules, epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, ejaculatory duct); paramesonephric duct → female tract, regresses in males
  • TDF drives sex cords deep → testis cords → seminiferous tubules at puberty

Descent of the testes

  • By month 9 the testes reach the scrotum (gubernaculum regression + ↑ intra-abdominal pressure); processus vaginalis closes above to leave the tunica vaginalis
  • Testes bring their innervation, blood supply and lymphatics from the posterior abdominal wall

blocks.html:
Direct measurement of GFR
  • The ideal marker is freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the tubules, and not metabolised or produced by the kidney. Only inulin meets all three
  • Renal clearance = the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per minute: CX = (UX × V) / PX, where UX = urine concentration, V = urine flow, PX = plasma concentration
  • For a marker meeting the three rules, clearance = GFR; infusing inulin for every patient is impractical, so surrogates are used
  • Normal eGFR is about 100-120 mL/min (CKD stages are in the CKD note)

BUN:creatinine ratio (non-GFR estimate)
  • Calculate with BUN in mmol/L and Cr in µmol/L: multiply BUN by 1000, then divide by Cr
  • > 80 → ↓ effective circulating volume (volume contraction or poor cardiac function)
  • Mechanism: in volume contraction urea is reabsorbed (ADH-mediated, follows Na) but creatinine is not, so urea rises out of proportion and gives a false impression of kidney damage

blocks.html:
• Creatinine clearance overestimates GFR (15–25% tubular secretion); inulin = gold standard
  • CKD-EPI underestimates GFR >60; cystatin C more accurate in children

lectures.framing: How kidney function is measured and investigated. The page runs from GFR markers (inulin, BUN, creatinine, iohexol, cystatin C) to non-GFR estimates (BUN:Cr ratio, urinalysis), then imaging and biopsy. The organising idea is the ideal marker: freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted, not made or metabolised by the kidney. Only inulin qualifies, so every bedside test is a trade-off against it.
lectures.keypoints: Inulin clearance = GFR (gold standard). Creatinine (normal 50-115 µmol/L) is poor for early disease: it barely rises until 40-50% of GFR is lost, and 15-25% is secreted, so creatinine clearance overestimates GFR (cimetidine and trimethoprim block that secretion). CKD-EPI is the most accurate estimate but cannot be used in AKI and underestimates GFR > 60; Cockcroft-Gault fails in obese and underweight patients. Cystatin C is standard of care in pediatrics. BUN:Cr > 80 (BUN × 1000) = ↓ effective circulating volume. RBC casts → glomerular, WBC casts → interstitial. Ultrasound is the commonest renal imaging test, CT is gold standard for stones, and biopsy is for unexplained decline with heavy hematuria and heavy proteinuria.

Nephrotic syndrome (non-proliferative glomerular disease)
  • Criteria: proteinuria > 3.5 g/day, edema, hypoalbuminemia (< 30 g/L), hyperlipidemia, lipiduria
  • Edema from ↓ oncotic pressure; hyperlipidemia because the liver ↑ albumin synthesis and makes lipoproteins with it
  • Adults: rule out secondary causes, then biopsy for the primary cause
  • Children: no biopsy, since most have minimal change disease. MCD: EM shows podocyte effacement (loss of charge barrier); Tx prednisone; biopsy only if steroid-resistant

blocks.html:
Gross hematuria
  • Brown or red urine; 1 mL of blood changes the colour, so exclude contamination (menstruation, post-partum)
  • Always do urinalysis + microscopy: colour mimics include hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria, beeturia and phenazopyridine
  • Always ask about a bleeding diathesis (anticoagulants, coagulopathy): it unmasks structural lesions and affects biopsy

Microscopy, DRE/PSA, US or CT, urine cytology, cystoscopy (bladder cancer, especially older adults)

blocks.html:
Nephritic syndrome (proliferative glomerular disease)
  • Criteria: RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs, moderate proteinuria, ↓ GFR, hypertension
  • Treatment: high-dose prednisone + IV cyclophosphamide; if no response, rituximab and plasmapheresis (varies by condition)
  • Other causes from the lecture: children, IgA vasculitis and HUS (most after E. coli O157:H7); adults, infective endocarditis, cryoglobulinemia, MPGN
