blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Dipstick detects ≥300 mg/day, misses immunoglobulins → UPEP for light chains
  • ACR: microalbuminuria 2–20 mg/mmol (dipstick negative); macro >20
  • Orthostatic proteinuria (adolescents) = benign
  • Nephrotic: >3.5 g/day, ↓ albumin, edema, lipids; MCD (children), membranous (Caucasian adults), FSGS (Black patients)
  • Child with nephrotic syndrome → prednisone without biopsy; adult → biopsy
  • Hematuria ≥3 RBC/HPF; glomerular = >70% dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, protein >1 g/day
  • RPGN (crescents) → high-dose steroids + IV cyclophosphamide/rituximab ± plasmapheresis

lectures.framing: Proteinuria and hematuria are the cardinal manifestations of renal disease. Each is worked up the same way: detect and quantify, then classify, and the key split in both is glomerular vs non-glomerular. Heavy glomerular proteinuria leads to the nephrotic syndrome; glomerular hematuria with casts leads to the nephritic syndrome.
lectures.keypoints: Normal: protein < 150 mg/day, < 3 RBC/hpf. 24-h urine is the gold standard for protein; the dipstick misses immunoglobulins and proteinuria < 300 mg/day, so use the urine albumin/Cr ratio (microalbuminuria 2-20 mg/mmol). Transient and orthostatic proteinuria are benign; persistent proteinuria is pathologic (diabetes most common). Overflow proteinuria (myeloma light chains) needs serum and urine electrophoresis. Glomerular hematuria = dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, protein > 1 g/day; urinary tract hematuria = monomorphic RBCs, no casts → imaging, cytology, cystoscopy. The dipstick also reads myoglobin and hemoglobin, so confirm with microscopy. Nephrotic: > 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminemia, edema, lipids; children → prednisone without biopsy (minimal change), adults → biopsy. RPGN (crescents) is an emergency: high-dose steroids + IV cyclophosphamide.

lectures.name: Acute Kidney Injury
lectures.title: Acute Kidney Injury

blocks.alt: acute kidney injury overview.svg

blocks.html:
Definition and epidemiology
  • Acute ↑ in creatinine: ↑ 44 µmol/L, or > 50% above baseline, or 50% ↓ in calculated CrCl. Interpret Cr for age, weight and sex (muscle mass)
  • CKD-EPI and other creatinine equations assume a steady state, so they are invalid in AKI; nuclear GFR scans or cystatin C are more accurate
  • 5% of hospitalised and 20% of ICU patients (multi-organ dysfunction)
  • Mortality 7-80%, driven by the underlying disease; deaths mostly from sepsis, cardiac and respiratory failure. Worse with oliguria (< 400 mL/day)

Obstruction of both outflow tracts (or of a solitary kidney)

Cardiogenic shock, CHF, massive PE, tamponade

Postrenal AKI
  • Suspect with sudden onset of anuria
  • Causes: BPH, prostate and cervical cancer, stones, strictures, retroperitoneal fibrosis
  • Bladder catheterisation and renal US; Foley to relieve; nephrostomy or ureteric stents if the block is above the bladder
  • Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and hemorrhagic cystitis

blocks.html:
Acute tubular necrosis
  • Most common cause of AKI in hospitalised patients (ischemic > nephrotoxic)
  • Phases: initiation (hours-days of injury) → maintenance (days-weeks; GFR and urine output lowest) → recovery (post-ATN diuresis; uremia and hypovolemia may persist; most recover by 6 weeks)
  • Pathophysiology: loss of tubular cell polarity and brush border → cell death and sloughing into the lumen → granular casts
  • Ischemic ATN: anything that causes prerenal AKI, plus renal vasoconstrictors (cyclosporine, NE, epinephrine, amphotericin B), DIC, hyperviscosity, COX inhibitors
  • Nephrotoxic ATN: exogenous (aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, contrast, cyclosporine, tacrolimus, acyclovir, cisplatin, methotrexate, foscarnet) or endogenous (myoglobin, hemoglobin, crystals, myeloma light chains)

Acute interstitial nephritis
  • Tubules and interstitium filled with lymphocytes, usually a drug reaction
  • Drugs: antibiotics (penicillins 30%), sulfa drugs, NSAIDs, PPIs, allopurinol
  • Not dose-dependent: can take weeks (up to 18 months for NSAIDs); much faster on re-exposure (3-5 days)
  • Signs: fever, serum eosinophilia, maculopapular rash
  • Other causes: infection (strep, Legionella, CMV), autoimmune (sarcoidosis, TINU), idiopathic
  • Most fully recover within 1 year

rows: Most common GN worldwide, especially in Asians
Recurrent sinusitis, joint pain, petechial rash, pulmonary hemorrhage
blocks.lead: Glomerulonephritis: 5 shared criteria (hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts, proteinuria < 3 g/day, ↑ Cr, hypertension, oliguria)

blocks.title: RPGN
blocks.html: Crescentic GN: crescents in Bowman's space from severe inflammation. An emergency: high-dose prednisone + cyclophosphamide + plasmapheresis to avoid dialysis.

Indications for dialysis: AEIOU
  • Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia), Ischemia or ingestion of a drug, Overload of fluid, Uremia
  • Uremic symptoms: fatigue, pruritus, N/V, anorexia, platelet dysfunction
  • Emergency indications: asterixis, seizures, uremic encephalopathy, uremic pericarditis

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• AKI: ↑ Cr 44 or >50% from baseline, or CrCl ↓ 50%
  • Sudden anuria → postrenal; renal U/S for hydronephrosis
  • Prerenal: hyaline casts, low urine Na/FENa, BUN:Cr >80; ATN: muddy brown granular casts
  • AIN: drug hypersensitivity, not dose-dependent, fever/eosinophilia/rash, sterile pyuria + WBC casts
  • Atheroemboli after catheterization: livedo, purple toes; Cr does not improve with IV fluids
  • Urgent dialysis: AEIOU (acidosis, hyperK⁺, ingestion, overload, uremia)

lectures.framing: AKI is an acute (hours to weeks) rise in serum creatinine. The approach is a sequence: rule out prerenal and postrenal first (they are the easiest: volume status and urine Na, then renal ultrasound), then sort intrinsic AKI by compartment: tubule (ATN), interstitium (AIN), glomerulus (GN), vessels (atheroemboli).
lectures.keypoints: AKI = Cr ↑ 44 µmol/L or > 50% from baseline, or CrCl ↓ 50%; creatinine-based GFR equations are invalid in AKI. Prerenal: urine Na < 20, FENa < 1%, BUN:Cr > 80, hyaline casts (normal). Intrinsic: FENa > 2%, muddy brown granular casts in ATN. Postrenal: sudden anuria, hydronephrosis on US, bland sediment → Foley. ATN is the most common hospital AKI (ischemic > nephrotoxic); clinical diagnosis, supportive care. AIN: drugs (penicillins, sulfa, NSAIDs, PPIs, allopurinol), not dose-dependent, fever + eosinophilia + rash, WBC casts and urine eosinophils; stop the drug. Atheroemboli after catheterization: diagnosis of exclusion, never biopsy, Cr does not improve with IV fluids. Dialysis: AEIOU; asterixis, seizures, uremic encephalopathy and pericarditis are emergencies.

lectures.name: Chronic Kidney Disease
lectures.title: Chronic Kidney Disease

blocks.alt: chronic kidney disease overview.svg

blocks.html:
Definition, pathology and epidemiology
  • Kidney damage or eGFR < 60 for ≥ 3 months, not treated with dialysis or transplant. Significant CKD also includes eGFR ≥ 60 with proteinuria, hematuria or anatomic abnormalities
  • Pathology (biopsy not used for diagnosis): hyaline nodules in glomeruli, leathery granular cortex, renal artery stenosis, small shrunken kidneys
  • Rising with an ageing population; causes diabetic nephropathy > HTN > glomerulonephritis; polycystic kidney disease = most common genetic cause of ESRD (large cystic kidneys)
  • Associated with CVD, CHF, PVD and stroke; lower GFR = higher mortality, mostly cardiovascular
  • Stage with eGFR (best is CKD-EPI) interpreted for age: eGFR peaks at 40 then falls 0.7-1 mL/min/year

blocks.lead: CKD stages (well managed patients may stabilise at stages 1-2; stages 3-4 carry the greatest risk of progression)

blocks.html:
Why CKD progresses: the hyperfiltration cycle
  1. Nephrons are lost; surviving glomeruli must filter the same blood volume (hyperfiltration)
  2. ↑ glomerular capillary pressure (glomerular hypertension)
  3. Basement membrane damage → proteinuria → tubulointerstitial inflammation → scarring
  4. More scarring → ↑ blood pressure → the cycle continues

Hence hypertension is a key risk factor for progression, and below ~25% of normal GFR decline continues regardless of the original insult.

rows: 1. Stop or slow GFR decline. 2. Prevent additional damage. 3. Maintain nutrition. 4. Prevent or limit uremic complications

blocks.html:
• CKD = damage or eGFR <60 for ≥3 months, not on dialysis/transplant

  • Slow progression: ACEi/ARB, BP, lipids, glycemia; avoid NSAIDs/aminoglycosides/contrast

lectures.framing: CKD is defined by damage or eGFR < 60 for ≥ 3 months and staged by GFR. The core concept is the hyperfiltration cycle, which makes CKD self-perpetuating once enough nephrons are lost. Management follows from it: slow GFR decline, prevent further hits, manage uremic complications, and plan renal replacement early.
lectures.keypoints: CKD = kidney damage or eGFR < 60 for ≥ 3 months, not on dialysis or transplant. Causes: diabetic nephropathy > HTN > GN (PKD is the commonest genetic cause of ESRD). Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death. eGFR falls 0.7-1 mL/min/year after 40, so < 60 may be normal for age but < 30 is abnormal at any age. Once GFR is < 25% of normal it keeps falling even if the insult is removed. Slow progression with ACEi/ARB (if not volume contracted) and strict BP control, protein restriction if on a high-protein diet, lipids and glucose (HbA1c < 7%); avoid NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, volume depletion, UTI, obstruction and pregnancy. Uremia appears at stages 4-5.

lectures.name: Diabetic Nephropathy
lectures.title: Diabetic Nephropathy

blocks.html:
Epidemiology
  • T1DM onset is clear-cut (polyuria, polydipsia), so its renal course is well described; renal risks are the same in T1DM and T2DM
  • 25-45% of T1DM patients develop nephropathy, and 8-20% of those reach ESRD after 20 years; falling with better glucose and BP control and ACEi
  • Higher risk in Indigenous, South Asian and African populations

Pathology and natural history
  • Driven by hyperglycemia and hypertension
  • Sequence: mesangial expansion (glycosylated proteins, inflammation) → GBM thickening → glomerular sclerosis
  • Scarring from advanced glycosylation end products, promoted by angiotensin II, TGF-β, VEGF and protein kinase C; arteriolosclerosis adds ischemic injury
  • Course: diabetes → rising BP and microalbuminuria → proteinuria and rising Cr → ESRD
  • GFR first rises (hyperfiltration): hyperglycemia causes afferent vasodilation and intraglomerular hypertension (IGF-1, ANP, sex hormones); it then falls

rows: Blood pressure, GFR and intraglomerular pressure, glycemic control, microalbuminuria

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Earliest DN = microalbuminuria (30–300 mg/day)
  • Targets: A1C ≤7%, BP <130/80, ACEi/ARB
  • ACEi/ARB → efferent dilation; SGLT2i → afferent constriction; both ↓ intraglomerular pressure

lectures.framing: Diabetic nephropathy is the commonest cause of CKD. The page follows its natural history: hyperfiltration → microalbuminuria → overt proteinuria → rising Cr → ESRD. The organising idea is that microalbuminuria is the earliest detectable, still reversible stage, so screening by urine albumin/Cr ratio and early ACEi plus glycemic and BP control decide the outcome.
lectures.keypoints: Renal risk is the same in T1DM and T2DM; nephropathy peaks 10-15 years after T1DM onset, and no proteinuria after 20 years means only 1%/year risk. Microalbuminuria (30-300 mg/day, ACR 2-20) = early nephropathy and is missed by the dipstick; macroalbuminuria > 300 mg/day (ACR > 20). Progression to overt proteinuria occurs in < 50%. Treat with HbA1c < 7%, BP < 130/80, ACEi/ARB (efferent dilation) and SGLT2 inhibitors (afferent constriction; not in T1DM); LDL < 2. Screen T1DM from 5 years after diagnosis, T2DM at diagnosis, then yearly ACR. Microalbuminuria → start ACEi even if normotensive.

lectures.name: Kidney Transplantation
lectures.title: Kidney Transplantation

blocks.html:
Why and how
  • Best treatment for ESRD: ↑ survival and QOL vs dialysis; living > deceased donor (15-20 vs 10-12 years); pre-emptive transplant (before dialysis) has better outcomes
  • Matched by blood type: type O donors can give to anyone; type AB recipients can receive from anyone
  • Past transfusions, pregnancies and transplants expose patients to HLA antigens → ↑ panel reactive antibody (PRA) → more rejection and more immunosuppression needed
  • Donor and recipient are tested for CMV and EBV (EBV can cause lymphoma under immunosuppression)
  • No immunosuppression needed only for identical twins
  • History: 1954 first transplant; 1960s azathioprine + prednisone; 1970s ATG induction; 1980s cyclosporine (revolutionised survival); 1990s on MMF and tacrolimus, 1-year graft survival 90%

blocks.html:
• Transplant = best survival + QoL of RRT

lectures.framing: Transplant is the best treatment for ESRD. The page covers who gets which kidney (ABO, HLA and PRA), the immunosuppressive drugs and their toxicities, and the types of rejection with their treatment. Post-transplant problems are approached like any kidney problem: prerenal or postrenal first, then intrinsic or transplant-specific.
lectures.keypoints: Transplant improves survival and QOL over dialysis; living donor grafts last 15-20 years vs 10-12 for deceased, and pre-emptive transplant does best. Prior transfusions, pregnancies and transplants ↑ PRA and rejection risk. Maintenance = prednisone + CNI (tacrolimus) + MMF (MMF → azathioprine in pregnancy). CNIs are nephrotoxic and CYP3A4-metabolised: anti-epileptics ↓ levels; verapamil, diltiazem, erythromycin, azoles ↑ levels. Avoid allopurinol with azathioprine. Acute rejection is mostly cell-mediated and needs a biopsy: pulse IV steroids + switch cyclosporine → tacrolimus; add thymoglobulin if vascular; plasmapheresis/IVIG only for antibody-mediated rejection. Chronic rejection (interstitial fibrosis) has no cure: control BP, glucose, lipids.

lectures.name: Diuretics
lectures.title: Diuretics
lectures.framing: Diuretics ↑ urine volume by blocking electrolyte (mainly NaCl) reabsorption. They are organised by nephron site, and the share of Na reabsorbed at that site predicts potency: PCT 65% > loop of Henle 15-25% > DCT 4-10% > collecting duct 2-5%. The page summarises all five classes, then compares the three main ones (thiazide, loop, K+-sparing) side by side.
lectures.keypoints: Loop diuretics (TAL, NKCC2): most potent, used for edema, work even with impaired renal function, ↓ Ca2+ and Mg2+, ototoxic; all sulfa except ethacrynic acid. Thiazides (DCT, NCC): moderate effect, first-line for HTN (vasodilation), ↑ Ca2+ (good for osteoporosis and calcium stones; can mask hypercalcemia of malignancy or hyperPTH), ↑ glucose, lipids, uric acid; long-acting thiazide-like agents (chlorthalidone) cut CV events more. Loop and thiazide → hypokalemia + alkalosis; K+-sparing → hyperkalemia + acidosis (avoid in renal failure and with K+ supplements, ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs). Spironolactone is antiandrogenic, eplerenone is not. All diuretics are contraindicated in anuria.

↑ tubular osmotic pressure draws water into the lumen
Block ENaC or the mineralocorticoid receptor
Combined with others to spare K+

blocks.html:
Why loop diuretics cause so much hypokalemia
  1. ↓ K+ reabsorption through the blocked NKCC2
  2. More Na+ reaches the collecting duct → ↑ ENaC activity → ↑ K+ secretion
  3. Volume contraction → ↑ aldosterone → further ↑ K+ secretion

This is why K+-sparing agents are added to prevent K+ wasting.

weeks.label: Week 16 - Urinary Infection, Obstruction & Urologic Malignancy

lectures.name: Urinary Tract Infections
lectures.title: Urinary Tract Infections

blocks.alt: urinary tract infection overview.svg

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Dysuria: burning, tingling or stinging of the urethra and meatus with voiding, often with frequency and urgency
  • Organisms: E. coli 80-90%; also Enterococcus, GBS, Staph. saprophyticus, Klebsiella, Proteus
  • Common DDx: acute simple cystitis (= acute uncomplicated UTI = bladder infection). Less common: complicated UTI, urethritis, BPH, foreign body, interstitial cystitis, dermatologic conditions, urethral stricture, drugs, vulvovaginal cancer, bicycle or horseback riding
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: positive culture without symptoms. Very common in the elderly (25-50% of women, 12-25% of men). Leave untreated except in pregnancy (untreated → pyelonephritis) or before a urologic procedure
  • Recurrent UTI: 2 uncomplicated UTIs in 6 months or 3 positive cultures in 12 months

rows: UTI vs a rarer cause of dysuria: hematuria, discharge, flank pain, fever, malaise, previous episodes, allergies, sexual partners, systemic or skin symptoms. Recurrent UTI: past cultures with sensitivities, imaging, link to sex. Men: perineal pain, cloudy urine, prostate issues, partners
Often unnecessary; vitals, abdomen, CVA tenderness. Bimanual exam if heavy discharge or dyspareunia; LTC: add GU, neuro, respiratory, ENT; men: DRE and genital inspection

Urinalysis: leukocytes + nitrites suggest UTI
Culture not needed for straightforward cystitis in women or asymptomatic bacteriuria in the elderly; do it for repeated dysuria, broad DDx, elderly, men, recurrent UTI
Men with dysuria: NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea, PSA

1st line: nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID x 5 d, fosfomycin 3 g once, TMP/SMX 160/800 mg BID x 3 d
2nd line: amoxicillin, norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin; 3rd line: cephalexin, levofloxacin

Treat, then test of cure by culture. Fluoroquinolones contraindicated throughout; TMP/SMX and nitrofurantoin avoided in the 1st trimester and > 36 wk. Good choices: amoxicillin, cephalexin 500 mg q6h x 7 d, nitrofurantoin, TMP/SMX

No treatment for bacteriuria without urinary symptoms. Visit the patient; culture if prescribing. Still mostly E. coli but resistance ↑: avoid TMP/SMX; nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin; treat 7 d. Delirium or agitation is often wrongly blamed on bacteriuria: look for non-infectious causes

Treat 7 d with a different agent the last culture was sensitive to, or the same agent for longer. Prophylaxis: ↑ water intake; post-coital nitrofurantoin or TMP/SMX if linked to sex. Consider GU ultrasound

Main DDx: simple cystitis vs complicated UTI; always culture. Complicated: 7 d if mild, 14 d if severe ± IV
1st line oral: TMP/SMX, nitrofurantoin, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin; IV: ampicillin + gentamicin or tobramycin
2nd line IV: cefotaxime, ceftriaxone, cipro, levo, pip-tazo; 3rd line: ceftazidime, imipenem, meropenem
TMP/SMX, clindamycin, cephalosporins ineffective; use amoxicillin or nitrofurantoin
Fosfomycin, ampicillin, nitrofurantoin ineffective; use amox-clav or TMP/SMX
Not susceptible to fosfomycin, TMP/SMX, nitrofurantoin or ampicillin

blocks.title: Complicated is a clinical call
blocks.html: Men do not automatically have complicated UTIs. Complicated = fever, chills, fatigue, flank pain, CVA tenderness, perineal pain in men, uncontrolled diabetes, immunosuppression. Pregnancy and renal transplant need special management; always factor in regional resistance (SW Ontario, LTC homes).

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Uncomplicated cystitis: no culture needed; nitrofurantoin 5 d, TMP/SMX 3 d, or fosfomycin 3 g once
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat in pregnancy (e.g., cephalexin 7 d); not in LTC patients without urinary symptoms
  • Men: culture, treat ≥7 d; complicated = immunosuppressed, uncontrolled DM, structural, fever/flank pain

lectures.framing: Dysuria is usually simple cystitis, but the job is to decide who needs more than a short empiric course. The page defines the terms (asymptomatic bacteriuria, recurrent, reinfection vs relapse), gives the general approach, then treats each population separately: adult women, pregnancy, long-term care, recurrent UTI and men.
lectures.keypoints: E. coli causes 80-90%. Simple cystitis needs no culture: nitrofurantoin 100 mg BID x 5 d, TMP/SMX BID x 3 d, or fosfomycin 3 g once. Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before a urologic procedure; never in LTC residents without urinary symptoms (delirium is not a UTI). Pregnancy: no fluoroquinolones; avoid TMP/SMX and nitrofurantoin in the 1st trimester and > 36 wk; test of cure. Reinfection > 2 wk, different organism; relapse < 2 wk, same organism. Complicated UTI is defined by features (fever, flank pain, CVA tenderness, DM, immunosuppression), not by sex: 7 d mild, 14 d severe.

lectures.name: Urinary Tract Obstruction
lectures.title: Urinary Tract Obstruction

blocks.alt: urinary tract obstruction overview.svg

blocks.html:
Definitions
  • Uremia: clinical features of renal failure (fluid overload, hyperkalemia, confusion, pericarditis); azotemia = ↑ BUN
  • Obstructive uropathy: reversible or irreversible renal impairment from obstructed drainage
  • Hydronephrosis: dilated renal pelvis and calyces; may be obstruction, or VUR or megaureter. Seen on US, IVP or CT
  • Renal colic: acute ureteral obstruction by a stone. Unilateral, severe, persistent with waves; flank radiating to scrotum or labia. Once the stone reaches the bladder it passes easily (ureter is much narrower than the urethra)
  • Urinary retention: acute or chronic inability to void; painful, palpable, distended bladder. Usually men with BPH; also prostate cancer, stricture, neurogenic. Diagnosed clinically, no imaging needed. Chronic retention → trabeculated bladder, diverticula, hydronephrosis
  • Calyceal diverticulum: urine-filled cavity off a calyx; often holds stones and obstructs a single calyx

Causes
  • Congenital or acquired, benign or malignant, unilateral or bilateral, intrinsic or extrinsic; at the calyces, pelvis, ureter or bladder outlet
  • Congenital: duplicated pelvis, UPJ obstruction, calyceal cysts, vascular anomalies, horseshoe kidney
  • UPJ obstruction: aperistaltic proximal ureter segment; congenital or functional
  • Ureteral duplication: the upper-pole ureter inserts lower on the bladder; below the external sphincter → continuous incontinence in children

rows: Collecting-system pressure ↑ (normal 6-7 mmHg, up to 50-70); prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation → ↑ RBF to hold GFR
Blood shunted to the vasa recta → medullary washout → can't concentrate urine (drives post-obstructive diuresis)
Afferent vasoconstriction (Ang II, thromboxane A2) → RBF falls below baseline, ureteral pressure falls

blocks.html:
• First derangement: loss of concentrating ability (tubular damage → can't excrete K⁺ or fully acidify urine)
  • Glomerular function is spared until later
  • Other sequelae: stones, UTI, sepsis (antibiotics don't work in the presence of obstruction)

rows: Clinical: flank pain or colic, retention or overflow incontinence, anuria, oliguria, uremia, stones, recurrent UTI
BUN and Cr ↑ only with bilateral obstruction (the other kidney compensates); urine Na⁺ higher in prerenal than postrenal
Renal US first; IVP (not if Cr > 200); retrograde pyelogram; Lasix renogram (nuclear scan of split function and some causes)
Correct acid-base and electrolytes; dialyze if needed

Bladder outlet: Foley (suprapubic if many strictures)
Renal or ureteral: ureteral stent (internal) or percutaneous nephrostomy (external)

BPH: α-blocker or finasteride, or TURP
Stone: ESWL (easy, lower success), ureteroscopy, percutaneous removal

blocks.title: Post-obstructive diuresis
blocks.html:
> 150 mL/h after relief of complete bilateral obstruction (not unilateral). Excess urea and water plus ongoing Na⁺ and electrolyte loss until concentrating ability returns; usually self-limiting but can be life-threatening. Rarely DI-like salt and water loss → hypovolemia.

Manage: hourly urine output, vitals, electrolytes (especially K⁺), daily weight. Most patients drink to replace losses; if output > 200 mL/h, give normal saline at 50% of the previous hour's output ± K⁺.

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Retention: urethral catheter first
  • Post-obstructive diuresis after relief of bilateral/bladder-outlet obstruction; usually mild, self-limiting

lectures.framing: Obstruction anywhere from calyx to urethra raises back-pressure on the kidney; the injury is ultimately ischemic, and the first function lost is concentrating ability. The page defines the presentations (renal colic, retention, hydronephrosis), walks the biphasic blood-flow response, then the approach: diagnose, decompress, fix the cause, and watch for post-obstructive diuresis.
lectures.keypoints: Hydronephrosis does not always mean obstruction (VUR, megaureter). Early: prostaglandin afferent dilation ↑ RBF; after ~6 h: Ang II and thromboxane A2 constrict → ↓ RBF → ischemia. First loss is concentrating ability (and K⁺ excretion). Irreversible loss after 6-8 weeks; complete, bilateral and infected obstruction are worse, and infection behind an obstruction is an emergency (antibiotics alone fail). BUN/Cr ↑ only if bilateral. Renal US first. Decompress: Foley for bladder outlet, stent or nephrostomy above. Post-obstructive diuresis > 150 mL/h after relief of bilateral obstruction.

lectures.name: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia
lectures.title: Benign Prostate Disorders: Prostatitis and BPH

blocks.alt: benign prostatic hyperplasia overview.svg

blocks.html:
Prostate gland
  • Accessory sex gland secreting lipids, proteases, zinc and citrate for sperm survival
Prostatitis
  • Inflammatory syndromes of the prostate (female counterpart: interstitial cystitis); most common urologic diagnosis in men < 50
  • Categories: I acute bacterial and II chronic bacterial (both rare; Enterobacteriaceae and enterococci); IIIa chronic pelvic pain syndrome (most common): dysfunctional voiding, non-nociceptive pain, intraprostatic ductal reflux; IIIb asymptomatic inflammation
  • Diagnosis: Hx and PEx with DRE, urinalysis and culture, cytology, semen cultures, residual urine; rarely cystoscopy. Bacterial prostatitis is confirmed by cultures before and after prostatic massage (Meares-Stamey 4-glass: prostatic samples ≥ 10x urethral or bladder counts)

rows: Sudden dysuria, urgency, frequency; fever, occasional sepsis; perineal, pelvic or suprapubic pain; retention. May form a prostatic abscess (septic or immunosuppressed; needs transurethral or IR drainage)
IV ampicillin + gentamicin until afebrile, then 4 wk quinolone
Recurrent UTIs or prior acute infection; chronic dysuria, urgency, frequency
Perineal, low back or scrotal pain > 3 months, often post-ejaculation; urinary symptoms incl. hesitancy; negative cultures, no objective findings
α-blockers, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, pelvic floor physiotherapy (try before meds or surgery)

blocks.html:
BPH basics
  • Men > 50: > 50% by 60 y, 90% by 85 y; LUTS ↓ quality of life and sleep
  • No need to treat mild or moderate symptoms medically unless the patient is bothered
  • 5-ARI + α-blocker combination best reduces symptoms and retention; PDE5 inhibitors also help BPH-LUTS

blocks.alt: BPH treatment algorithm by symptom severity, bother and prostate size
blocks.cap: Mild or unbothered symptoms: watch and wait (add a 5-ARI if the prostate is large); bothersome moderate-severe symptoms: α-blocker or surgery for a small prostate, α-blocker and/or 5-ARI or surgery for a large one.

cols: Approach to the typical man with LUTS
rows:
Hx: FUNWISE (frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream, intermittency, straining, incomplete emptying) + bother; age > 50; prior UTI, retention, hematuria; meds (antihistamines, decongestants, diuretics, opiates, TCAs, caffeine); FHx incl. prostate cancer
PEx: DRE (size, nodularity, asymmetry, tenderness); abdomen (distended bladder, masses, hernia); genitalia (meatal stenosis, tight phimosis)
Urinalysis (exclude infection)

IPSS: FUNWISE + quality of life (frequent nocturia that doesn't bother him needs no drug)
Nocturnal polyuria: frequency-volume chart (24 h intake and output); if nocturia is the only symptom this is likelier than BPH
PSA: surrogate of prostate size (↑ PSA = ↑ volume); offer if life expectancy > 10 y and knowing about cancer would change management
Evening fluid restriction, diuretics in the morning, leg elevation (compression stockings), CPAP for OSA
Failed medical therapy, UTIs or hematuria; elevated PSA or abnormal DRE, or patient concern about cancer; any consecutive PSA rise from the new baseline after 6 months on a 5-ARI
Block α1 (NE) → relax prostate and bladder neck smooth muscle → ↑ flow
↓ testosterone → DHT → shrink prostate, ↓ PSA; best in large prostates
Dizziness, headache, postural hypotension, nasal congestion, asthenia, abnormal (retrograde) ejaculation; intraoperative floppy iris syndrome (screen for cataract surgery)
blocks.lead: Medical therapy (PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil also relax prostatic smooth muscle)

blocks.html:
Surgery
  • Absolute: urinary retention, renal failure from BPH or bladder outlet obstruction
  • Relative: recurrent infections, bladder stones, persistent prostatic bleeding, failed or intolerable meds, patient choice
  • TURP = gold standard: transurethral resection of the inner gland. Complications: retrograde ejaculation (> 75%); rarely ED, incontinence, regrowth (5-10%), bleeding, infection, stricture, bladder neck contracture; TURP syndrome (absorbed hypotonic irrigant → hyponatremia)
  • Alternatives: holmium laser ablation (HoLAP), transurethral vaporization (TUVP), photoselective vaporization (PVP)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Medical: α-blocker, 5-ARI, combination, PDE5i
  • Surgery if retention, stones, recurrent UTI/hematuria, upper-tract damage, or failed meds; TURP = gold standard

lectures.framing: Two benign prostate problems with different ages: prostatitis (the commonest urologic diagnosis under 50) and BPH (over 50). For BPH the organising idea is that bother, not symptoms alone, decides treatment, and prostate size decides the drug: α-blockers relax, 5-ARIs shrink.
lectures.keypoints: Prostatitis: IIIa chronic pelvic pain syndrome is most common (pain > 3 months, negative cultures; pelvic floor physio); acute bacterial = IV amp + gent then 4 wk quinolone; chronic bacterial = 6 wk quinolone. BPH LUTS = FUNWISE; IPSS includes QOL/bother. Nocturia alone → think nocturnal polyuria (frequency-volume chart). α-blockers: onset < 2 wk, hypotension, floppy iris syndrome. 5-ARIs: 3-6 months, best for large prostates, halve PSA. Combination is best. Absolute surgery indications: retention, renal failure from obstruction; TURP is gold standard (retrograde ejaculation > 75%). PSA rise on a 5-ARI → refer.

lectures.name: Prostate Cancer
lectures.title: Prostate Cancer

blocks.alt: prostate cancer overview.svg

blocks.html:
Basics
  • Most common non-cutaneous malignancy in men in North America; 3rd leading cause of cancer death in Canadian men; incidence ↑ but mortality ↓
  • Risk factors: age, androgens, FHx, African ancestry (possibly high-fat diet, vitamin D deficiency)
  • Adenocarcinoma, graded by Gleason (glandular differentiation): 4-6 well differentiated, 7 moderately, 8-10 anaplastic
  • Presentation: early disease is asymptomatic (found on PSA or a DRE nodule); advanced disease: bone pain, anemia, weight loss, fatigue
Screening
  • Goal: find disease at a curable stage. Offer PSA + DRE every 2 y for men 50-69; start at 45 if at increased risk
  • No routine screening under 50, over 70, or with life expectancy < 10 y; counsel men > 50 on risks and benefits (not all trials show ↓ prostate cancer mortality)

rows: False +: stones, scarring from surgery or infection. False −: small tumours, examiner skill
Screening, staging, prognosis, surveillance; no clear cut-off. PPV 30% if > 4, 45-60% if > 10 ng/mL
75% of cancers are found at PSA 4-10, mostly organ-confined and curable; > 10 more likely beyond the prostate
Cancer has more protein-bound PSA → lower free/total ratio
Concern if ≥ 0.5 ng/mL/yr with PSA < 4, or ≥ 1 ng/mL/yr with PSA > 4

blocks.html:
Screening dilemmas
  • 60 y, normal DRE, PSA 1.9 → 2.5 → 3.2: discuss biopsy risks and benefits; consider yearly PSA
  • 66 y, smooth 50 cc gland, PSA 6.6 (above the size-predicted PSA): counsel biopsy
  • 62 y, first PSA 27: repeat first (false positives happen); refer if still high
Diagnosis and staging
  • TRUS-guided biopsy is the only reliable diagnosis (imaging alone cannot diagnose); indicated for a palpable nodule or ↑ PSA. Risks: blood in urine, stool or semen, retention, infection (give prophylactic antibiotics)
  • Staging: DRE (palpable beyond the gland?), PSA > 50 = extraglandular spread, biopsy (grade, extracapsular extension); bone scan and CT abdomen/pelvis if higher risk. Most common metastatic site: bone
  • Prognosis: slow-growing; depends on grade, stage, treatment. Early well-differentiated disease after prostatectomy: > 95% 10-y survival; metastatic: < 10% 5-y survival. Treating a slightly raised PSA may not change lifespan: weigh the burden of diagnosis and procedures

rows: Active surveillance; radical prostatectomy; external beam radiotherapy; brachytherapy
Androgen deprivation; supportive (pain, bone health); chemo and immunotherapy for hormone-refractory disease
blocks.lead: Management by age, comorbidity, stage and grade (surgery and radiation have similar outcomes; involve urology and radiation oncology)

blocks.html:
Active surveillance (Gleason ≤ 6, low risk)
  • Monitor DRE, PSA and protocol biopsies; treat only if rapid PSA doubling, progression on DRE, grade progression, or ↑ tumour volume
  • Not the same as watchful waiting, which only treats once symptoms appear

rows: First choice for men < 70 with organ-confined cancer
Open, robotic or laparoscopic; removes gland + seminal vesicles + nodes. Transfusion, incontinence (4-16% at 1 y), ED (20-40%), infection, rectal injury. Biochemical recurrence: PSA > 0.2 ng/mL
Healthy, life expectancy > 10 y, prostate < 60 cc, good baseline urinary function
Outpatient seed implant via transrectal US, ~1 h, general or spinal. LUTS, pelvic pain, diarrhea, ED (30% long term), stricture, seed migration
No age, comorbidity or risk restrictions; good if not a surgical candidate
Daily for ~7 weeks; IBD and lupus are exclusions. Radiation proctitis and cystitis, ED, incontinence, hematuria, stricture, secondary bladder or rectal cancer. Recurrence: PSA ↑ 2 ng/mL

blocks.lead: PSA relapse after radical prostatectomy by grade

blocks.html:
Locally advanced or metastatic disease
  • Androgen deprivation: LHRH analogues, antiandrogens, orchidectomy
  • Supportive: NSAIDs, corticosteroids, radiation to painful bone mets
  • Bone health: bone scan to follow spread; bisphosphonates, calcium, vitamin D
Hormone-refractory disease
  • Docetaxel, abiraterone, enzalutamide, cabazitaxel
  • Immunotherapy: sipuleucel-T

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• TRUS-guided biopsy needed for diagnosis (palpable nodule or ↑ PSA); imaging alone not sensitive enough
  • Active surveillance for low-grade disease

lectures.framing: Prostate cancer is common and usually slow, so the lecture is about finding the curable ones without over-treating the rest. It runs screening (DRE, PSA and how to read it), diagnosis by TRUS biopsy, then management stratified by Gleason grade and stage: active surveillance, surgery or radiation for localized disease, androgen deprivation for advanced disease.
lectures.keypoints: Most common non-cutaneous cancer in North American men (lifetime 14%, death 3.5%). Screening: PSA + DRE every 2 y at 50-69 (from 45 if high risk); none < 50, > 70 or life expectancy < 10 y. PSA 4-10 is the curable grey zone; cancer has a lower free/total ratio and a faster rise. Biopsy is the only way to diagnose; PSA > 50 suggests spread; bone is the main metastatic site. Gleason ≤ 6: active surveillance; 8-10: multimodal. Radical prostatectomy for men < 70 with organ-confined disease; recurrence = PSA > 0.2 after surgery, ↑ 2 after radiation. Advanced: androgen deprivation.

lectures.name: Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses
lectures.title: Approach to Scrotal Pain and Masses

blocks.alt: scrotal pain and masses overview.svg

blocks.html:
Acute scrotal pain: history
  • Sudden vs gradual onset is the key question; duration, time course, aggravating and relieving factors (movement)
  • Associated UTI symptoms, recent trauma, previous similar episodes; PMHx, PSHx, meds, exposures

rows: Blood in the tunica vaginalis ± other scrotal spaces
Spermatic cord twists; congenital lack of gubernacular anchoring lets the testis lie horizontally and twist
Sudden severe pain; may have happened mildly before and untwisted
Gradual; UTI symptoms, fever, leukocytosis ± obstructive voiding
Rock-hard painful testis (venous outflow blocked); check the other side for horizontal lie
Swollen, firm, tender epididymis; testis non-tender or slightly tender
Depends on rupture; explore if expanding or ruptured
Surgery within 6-8 h; urgent referral to save the testis
Antibiotics; urgent referral unless the diagnosis is certain
blocks.lead: Acute scrotal pain (Ix for all: CBC, urinalysis, scrotal US with Doppler)

rows: Fluid around the testis. Infant: patent processus, communicating (drains) or not. Adult: fluid in the enclosed tunica vaginalis
Dilated pampiniform plexus from ↑ abdominal pressure or incompetent valves
Semen-filled sacs from a leak at the epididymis or rete testis
Usually left; asymptomatic or dull ache; found in infertility workup
Spherical or multilocular; feels like a third testicle
Varicocelectomy for severe pain or infertility
blocks.lead: Sub-acute scrotal pain and masses (scrotal US confirms, but Hx and PEx usually suffice)

blocks.title: Hernia or hydrocele?
blocks.html: Pinch above the swelling (the key test): you can get above a hydrocele but not above a hernia. Hernias may not transilluminate (solid contents), transmit a cough, and may have bowel sounds.

Varicocele on the right
  • A right-sided varicocele suggests retroperitoneal pathology compressing venous drainage: image it
Testicular cancer
  • Age 13-35; 1-2% of male cancers but 12% of cancer deaths at 20-36; highest in Scandinavia, rare in Asian and African populations; incidence doubled in 30 y
  • Average diagnostic delay 4-6 months
  • Presentation: painless firm enlargement, often found while washing; sometimes heavy ache, or gynecomastia and galactorrhea from β-hCG; abdominal mass from nodes; mets are the first presentation in 10-15% (abdomen, chest, liver, brain)
  • Risk factors: cryptorchidism (orchiopexy eases detection and partly lowers risk), atrophic or dysgenetic testis, prior contralateral cancer. Trauma is not a risk factor
  • Ix: tumour markers AFP, β-hCG; scrotal US; CT abdomen and chest for nodes and mets
  • Urologist: confirm, markers, radical orchiectomy (testis + spermatic cord), then stage-based surveillance ± chemo, node surgery or radiotherapy
  • Prognosis excellent; most metastatic disease is curable (chemo and radiation sensitive)

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Torsion: sudden, rock-hard testis, no Doppler flow → surgical emergency (6–8 h)
  • Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, tender epididymis, UTI signs/fever
  • Varicocele: left, bag of worms; right-sided → image the retroperitoneum
  • Spermatocele = "third testicle"; hydrocele transilluminates

lectures.framing: Sort the scrotum by tempo. Acute pain is hematocele, torsion or epididymo-orchitis, and the urgent question is torsion vs infection. Sub-acute pain or a mass is hydrocele, varicocele, spermatocele, hernia or testicular cancer, sorted at the bedside by transillumination, Valsalva and whether you can get above it.
lectures.keypoints: Torsion: sudden, rock-hard testis, contralateral horizontal lie, no Doppler flow → surgery within 6-8 h. Epididymo-orchitis: gradual, UTI symptoms, fever, tender epididymis, ↑ flow → antibiotics. Hydrocele transilluminates and you can get above it; a hernia you can't. Varicocele: left, bag of worms, ↑ with Valsalva; right-sided → look for retroperitoneal pathology. Spermatocele = third testicle. Testicular cancer: painless firm mass, age 13-35; markers AFP, β-hCG; radical (inguinal) orchiectomy; curable even when metastatic.

lectures.name: Approach to Renal Masses
lectures.title: Approach to Renal Masses
lectures.framing: Most renal masses are found incidentally on imaging, and most are not cancer. The page runs in the order you meet them: what kind of mass is it on imaging (simple cyst through solid enhancing), then how a small mass is staged and treated, the benign and malignant pathology, the hereditary syndromes, and finally metastatic RCC.
lectures.keypoints: Simple cyst and dromedary hump: no follow-up; refer everything else. Enhancement = > 20 HU; most solid enhancing masses are RCC; most fatty masses are angiomyolipomas (worry if > 4 cm or invasive). Small mass (≤ 4 cm): partial nephrectomy preferred; radical only for major vascular involvement or very large tumours. Clear cell (80-85%, PCT, VHL); chromophobe and oncocytoma arise from the DCT (BHD). mRCC spreads to lung, liver, lymph nodes, bone, brain; 20-30% present with mets. Paraneoplastic: SIADH, hypercalcemia, erythrocytosis, thrombocytosis.

blocks.html:
Differential of a renal mass
  • Infectious: abscess, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (XGP), TB, fungus
  • Infiltrative: sarcoidosis, endocrinopathies
  • Obstructive: hydronephrosis, congenital anomalies (e.g., horseshoe kidney)
  • Neoplastic: benign vs malignant; cystic
Renal neoplasms
  • Primary malignant: epithelial (renal cell, urothelial, SCC, collecting duct), stromal (liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, other sarcomas), hematogenous (lymphoma, leukemia)
  • Secondary: metastases
  • Benign: angiomyolipoma, oncocytoma, cortical adenoma

rows: How it was found (most are incidental), symptoms (constitutional, pain, hematuria), prior imaging; personal or family cancer history, obesity, HTN, medications (anticoagulants, antihypertensives), smoking, occupational carcinogens
Vitals, appearance and performance status, lymphadenopathy (cervical, inguinal); abdomen: flank bruising or discolouration, flank mass, tenderness, renal bruits

Imaging: CT abdomen/pelvis, MRI abdomen, renal US. CT or MRI is needed to fully characterize any mass that is not a simple cyst (shape, location, contour bulge, density vs kidney, enhancement)
Labs: CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, UA, urine culture, urine cytology
Cystoscopy if gross hematuria
Gross hematuria, microhematuria or abnormal cytology, any solid mass, pain with a mass, known hereditary kidney cancer carrier: i.e., everything except a simple cyst or a dromedary hump
Characterized on US: round, smooth borders, no nodules; single or multiple
Very common (40-60% of adults); no further testing or follow-up

Some component may be malignant (mostly low malignant potential)

Most are benign angiomyolipomas; concern if invasive or > 4 cm
Dromedary hump (splenic impression on the left kidney); collecting-system filling defect
Hump is benign; filling defect suggests urothelial carcinoma

blocks.html:
Small renal masses (≤ 4 cm)
  • Canadian guidelines: biopsy only if it will change management; partial nephrectomy preferred; radical nephrectomy if a partial is not feasible; thermal ablation + biopsy and active surveillance are options
  • Staging guides treatment and prognosis. Minimum workup: CT abdomen + pelvis, CXR or CT chest, liver enzymes, calcium and ALP (bone scan if abnormal or bone pain)
  • Biopsy: not always needed (diagnostic in 80-90%); indicated with a history of another cancer. Risks: tract seeding, bleeding
  • Localized kidney cancer is a surgical disease with cure as the goal; small tumours grow slowly with low metastatic potential, so elderly or comorbid patients can be followed
  • Radical nephrectomy (kidney outside Gerota's fascia ± adrenal): historical approach, now only for major vascular involvement or a very large tumour
  • Nephron-sparing (partial) nephrectomy: ideal for most small masses, and for a solitary kidney, bilateral multifocal tumours, CKD, diabetes or HTN. Robotic, with vascular occlusion then reconstruction; complications 10-25% (ischemia, hemorrhage, urine leak)
  • Thermal ablation (cryoablation, radiofrequency, microwave): kills but does not remove the mass; mostly percutaneous. Cryoablation freezes → coagulative necrosis

rows: Into renal vein or IVC below the diaphragm
N0 no nodes, N1 any regional node; M0 no mets, M1 mets
Most common benign mass (20% of people), < 1 cm, encapsulated grey-yellow, no clear cells; usually found at autopsy
Blood vessels + smooth muscle + fat; very common (F > M); may be symptomatic
Solid, enhancing, hard to tell from RCC on imaging; granular eosinophilic cells, central scar
5% of RCC; younger patients (F > M); very large but low metastatic potential; perinuclear halos

blocks.alt: Five H and E histology panels of renal tumours
blocks.cap: Left to right: clear cell RCC (clear glycogen-rich cytoplasm), papillary type 1, papillary type 2 (eosinophilic papillae), chromophobe (pale cells with perinuclear halos) and oncocytoma (granular pink cells).

rows: AD loss of a tumour suppressor on chromosome 3; VHL protein no longer binds ubiquitin ligase → ↑ angiogenesis and gluconeogenesis
Clear cell (VHL also mutated in sporadic clear cell)
Multi-organ: retinal, spinal, brain, inner ear, renal tumours
MET proto-oncogene → altered tyrosine kinase binding HGF → proliferation; all familial, only 13% of sporadic
AD loss of fumarate hydratase → shift to anaerobic metabolism
Aggressive papillary type 2 (metastasizes, not always multifocal)
Severe uterine fibroids and painful skin leiomyomas
blocks.lead: Hereditary kidney cancers (multiple, often bilateral tumours with a strong FHx)

blocks.html:
Who gets genetic testing (Canadian guidelines)
  • Bilateral or multifocal tumours, onset < 45 y, 1st or 2nd degree relative with renal cancer
  • Typical skin findings or associated tumours, early uterine fibroids, non-clear cell histology, or a known familial syndrome

Advanced (metastatic) RCC
  • Spreads to lung, liver, lymph nodes, bone, brain (3 L's, 2 B's)
  • Synchronous mets in 20-30% at presentation; mets can appear years after treating the primary (most in the first few years), driven by the primary's mutations
  • Prognosis (worse than non-metastatic): Motzer (low performance status, LDH > 1.5x, anemia, hypercalcemia, no prior nephrectomy) and Heng (performance status, time from diagnosis to mets, anemia, corrected Ca, platelets, neutrophils)
  • Paraneoplastic: SIADH (hyponatremia), hypercalcemia (PTH-like peptide or lytic bone mets), erythrocytosis (EPO), thrombocytosis
  • Treatment (usually fatal; minimize harm, maximize QOL): surgery for select patients or palliation (gross hematuria, bowel obstruction, low-volume mets); radiation for painful bone mets, CNS or soft tissue masses, local control; systemic therapy is key: immunotherapy (PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors), tyrosine kinase inhibitors (VEGF), plus bisphosphonates, opioids, steroids for appetite

lectures.name: Urothelial Cancer
lectures.title: Urothelial Cancer

rows: Often incidental; hematuria (gross or micro); less often clot colic, renal mass, pain, "UTI"; mets to lung, bone, nodes, liver; constitutional symptoms
Hematuria, often totally painless; dysuria, pain, UTI, abnormal cytology; less often mets, constitutional symptoms, local pressure
Age, smoking (+ second-hand), occupational carcinogens excreted in urine (petrol, leather, automotive, plastics, aniline and hair dyes), geographic (Balkan)
Same, plus prior chemo (cyclophosphamide), pelvic radiation, chronic infection or foreign body (catheter); FHx is not a recognized risk factor (except Lynch)
Remove the entire kidney + ureter (field effect); local resection if renal function is poor
By grade and stage: start with transurethral resection + staging imaging

blocks.html:
Reading hematuria
  • First confirm it is blood: red urine can be meds (phenazopyridine), beets, food colouring, concentrated urine, jaundice; or glomerular, vaginal, or worsened by anticoagulants
  • Initial → urethra; terminal → bladder neck or prostate; total → kidney or bladder; stringy clots → upper tract
  • Hematuria is not always cancer: BPH in older men, stones, UTI (uncommon), trauma, prior radiation or chemo, anticoagulants
  • Pain: intermittent with passing clots; or compression of nearby structures; back pain (retroperitoneal)
  • Index of suspicion: presenting complaint, age, male sex, smoking, urban > rural, pre-existing bladder disease, genetics (Lynch syndrome)

Investigations
  • Urinalysis (blood, infection) and cytology (detects high-grade UC; not useful during gross hematuria); CBC, creatinine, electrolytes
  • Renal US: hydronephrosis, stones, parenchymal mass
  • CT urogram (IVP outdated): filling defects and drainage
  • Cystoscopy: see and sample the bladder; stages and decides benign vs malignant
  • Field effect: all urothelium shares the carcinogen exposure, so the whole organ unit is removed for malignancy

blocks.title: Refer, don't re-treat
blocks.html: Refer to urology for gross hematuria, persistent microhematuria, or a renal mass. Assuming a UTI and treating with antibiotics again and again delays diagnosis.

rows: Superficial, low grade, single or infrequent recurrence (> 70% of bladder cancers are low grade)
Periodic cystoscopy; can recur as high grade
High grade, muscle-invasive, metastatic or locally advanced
Radical cystectomy + urinary diversion (ileal conduit, orthotopic neobladder, or continent pouch) or radiation ± chemo

blocks.html:
Bladder cancer treatments
  • Intravesical therapy: weekly immunotherapy (BCG) or chemo for 6 weeks for carcinoma in situ; ↓ recurrences
  • Radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive disease; diversion choice depends on age, health, preference, surgical factors
  • Radiotherapy (less effective) ± chemo (neoadjuvant, adjuvant, metastatic); immunotherapy
  • Invasive disease has a poorer outcome; distant mets can appear years after cystectomy

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Painless gross hematuria + smoking → urothelial cancer until proven otherwise
  • Work-up: urine microscopy ± cytology, CT (excretory phase), cystoscopy

lectures.framing: Urothelium lines everything from renal pelvis to urethra, and the same carcinogens bathe all of it. The presenting problem is hematuria, so the page starts with how to read hematuria, then compares upper tract vs bladder tumours, the shared workup (cystoscopy), and treatment shaped by the field effect and by grade and stage.
lectures.keypoints: Painless gross hematuria + smoking = urothelial cancer until proven otherwise. Risk: age, smoking (incl. second-hand), occupational dyes, petrol, leather, plastics; Balkan region; cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation. Contact time: bladder > renal pelvis > ureter > urethra. Stream timing: initial = urethra, terminal = bladder neck/prostate, total = kidney or bladder, stringy clots = upper tract. Cystoscopy decides benign vs malignant; cytology catches high grade. Field effect: upper-tract tumour → nephroureterectomy. Bladder: CIS → intravesical BCG; muscle-invasive → radical cystectomy + diversion. Don't treat hematuria as UTI repeatedly.

lectures.name: Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology
lectures.title: Special Issues in Pediatric Nephrology

blocks.lead: Pediatric BP thresholds (2017 AAP; by age, sex and height)

blocks.html:
Screening and measurement
  • All children > 3 y yearly; every visit (even < 3 y) if kidney disease, hyperthyroidism or BP-raising drugs (steroids)
  • Why: ↓ childhood CV morbidity, HTN tracks into adulthood, prevents emergencies (seizure, encephalopathy, heart failure). Prevalence ~5%, higher with obesity
  • Labile HTN (incl. white coat) is common: if > 90th percentile, re-measure twice and record the lower
  • Cuff by mid-arm circumference; confirm a high oscillometric reading by auscultation (thresholds are auscultatory)
  • Diagnose HTN only after elevated BP on 3 occasions, 1-2 weeks apart; in stage 2, assess for urgency or emergency at once

rows: Rule out white coat HTN with 24 h ABPM (also detects nocturnal and masked HTN); no meds or workup if white coat
Urgency (stage 2, asymptomatic) vs emergency (HTN-induced organ involvement: seizures, encephalopathy, heart failure, AKI)
Rule out secondary causes (CKD, renal artery stenosis, hyperthyroidism, Cushing) and target-organ damage (LVH)

Urgency: rapid correction to the 90th percentile; IV or oral, rapid onset (nifedipine, labetalol, hydralazine, minoxidil)
Emergency: ↓ 25% over 8 h, then to the 90th percentile over 26-48 h; IV, rapid onset, short acting (nitroprusside: cyanide risk; labetalol: caution in asthma, CHF, diabetes)
Non-pharmacologic first (salt restriction, weight control) for 6 months; oral meds if that fails, or at once if a secondary cause or LVH: CCB (amlodipine), ACEi, ARB, thiazide, β-blocker, α-blocker

blocks.html:
When to treat
  • Don't treat: BP from pain or stress, white coat, no repeat in the same visit (labile), or no repeat on 2+ occasions
  • Immediately (IV): stage 2 with emergency. ASAP (IV or oral): stage 2 with urgency. Early: stage 1 with target-organ damage, a secondary cause, or failed non-pharmacologic therapy
Approach to renal swelling (days)
  1. Rule out non-renal causes (CHF, liver disease, protein-losing enteropathy)
  2. Rule out AKI (↑ urea + creatinine)
  3. Nephrotic vs nephritic (proteinuria vs hematuria)
  4. Narrow the etiology by syndrome
  5. Confirm with clinical clues and targeted tests

rows: Injury → ↓ GFR → ↑ urea/Cr → oliguria → edema, electrolyte disturbance
Proteinuria → ↓ albumin → ↓ oncotic pressure → edema → oliguria
Inflammation → hematuria, slight proteinuria, ↓ GFR → oliguria → edema, HTN
Platelets + hemolysis (HUS); urine osm and Na (prerenal vs renal)

blocks.html:
AKI
  • Prerenal (↓ renal blood flow, e.g., dehydration): give fluid. Renal (ischemia, nephrotoxins, sepsis, GN): restrict fluid. Postrenal: obstruction
  • Diarrhea is a key cause in children: prerenal from hypovolemia, or renal from prolonged ischemia or HUS
AKI with diarrhea
  1. Confirm AKI (↑ urea and Cr)
  2. Rule out HUS: E. coli diarrhea → thrombotic microangiopathy → thrombocytopenia + hemolysis (↑ LDH, bilirubin, retics; ↓ Hb, haptoglobin; schistocytes)
  3. Prerenal vs ischemic renal by urine osmolality and Na
  4. Fluids for prerenal, restriction for renal

Treating AKI
  • Supportive: salt and fluid restriction, BP control, diuretics (furosemide, HCTZ)
  • Metabolic acidosis: often settles with rehydration; otherwise sodium bicarbonate
  • Hyperkalemia: calcium gluconate to protect the heart; shift K⁺ in (IV D5W + insulin, β2-agonist, NaHCO₃); Kayexalate to bind gut K⁺
  • Dialysis: no response to medical therapy (fluid, K⁺, acidosis despite hydration and NaHCO₃) or uremic complications (encephalopathy, pericarditis)

Nephrotic syndrome
  • Classic: edema, proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, hypercholesterolemia, normal Cr, usually normotensive
  • Causes: MCD (#1, 80-90%), FSGS (#2), mesangioproliferative, membranoproliferative and membranous GN. In adults membranous is most common, so adults are biopsied first
  • Options: (a) biopsy only if MCD is unlikely: age < 1 y, hematuria + HTN (FSGS), CKD, systemic autoimmune features (SLE, vasculitis), low C3 (MPGN); (b) steroids without biopsy (usual); FSGS is also treated as MCD at first; (c) supportive only (rarely, as spontaneous resolution is uncommon)
  • First episode: prednisone 60 mg/m²/d x 6 wk, then 40 mg/m² every 48 h x 6 wk. Relapse: 60 mg until protein negative or trace for 3 days, then 40 mg alternate days x 4 wk (shorter)

rows: ≥ 2 relapses within 6 months of presentation, or ≥ 4 in 12 months
Prevent relapse and steroid exposure: cyclophosphamide, MMF, rituximab, cyclosporine
2 consecutive relapses on alternate-day steroids or within 14 d of stopping

blocks.html:
Nephritic syndrome
  • Classic: recent ↓ urine output then edema, hematuria, mild proteinuria, HTN, normal or mildly ↑ urea and Cr
  • Causes: post-infectious (post-strep) GN (immune complex, anti-strep antibody), IgA nephropathy (immune complex, anti-glycosylated IgA), C3 glomerulopathy, membranoproliferative GN, Henoch-Schönlein purpura
  • Biopsy if: C3 still low at 6 weeks (confirms C3 GN), CKD develops in IgA nephropathy, or IgA presents with significant AKI
  • Treatment: supportive for fluid overload and HTN (salt restriction, antihypertensives, diuretics); unlike AKI, no dialysis, K⁺ or acidosis treatment needed. PSGN resolves spontaneously; IgA and C3 GN: monitor for CKD, biopsy if CKD, then steroids, MMF, azathioprine

rows: Recurrent; CKD in 33% (supportive if no CKD, immunosuppression if CKD)
Recurrent; higher CKD risk; recurs after transplant
blocks.lead: Nephritic syndrome with a sore throat: use C3

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html: • Nephrotic syndrome in a child → MCD → steroids without biopsy

lectures.framing: Two pediatric problems: hypertension (percentile-based diagnosis, then a protocol that depends on stage) and renal swelling. For edema, the organising idea is one key lab per syndrome: ↑ urea and creatinine means AKI, massive proteinuria means nephrotic, hematuria means nephritic, and the timing of edema vs oliguria tells them apart.
lectures.keypoints: HTN = ≥ 95th percentile; adolescent stage 1 is ≥ 130/80. Check BP yearly from age 3; diagnose only after 3 visits 1-2 wk apart. Stage 2: urgency vs emergency first; emergency → IV, ↓ 25% over 8 h. AKI: ↑ urea + Cr, edema follows oliguria; with diarrhea rule out HUS (↓ platelets + hemolysis); prerenal (↑ urine osm, ↓ Na → give fluid) vs renal (↓ osm, ↑ Na → restrict). Nephrotic: normal Cr, edema precedes oliguria; MCD → steroids without biopsy. Nephritic: hematuria; C3 sorts it: normal = IgA, low and normalizes by 6 wk = PSGN, stays low = C3 GN.

lectures.name: Special Issues in Pediatric Urology
lectures.title: Special Issues in Pediatric Urology

blocks.html:
Undescended testis (UDT)
  • Testis not in the scrotum: 3% of term boys (⅓ of preterm); most descend within 3-6 months
  • Risk factors: preterm, IUGR, twins, breech, FHx, IVF (anti-androgen exposure), flame retardants and fluorocarbons
  • Hx: birth history, episodes of acute scrotum, was it ever descended (congenital vs secondary ascent)
  • PEx step 1, retractile? A retractile testis (active cremasteric reflex) can be brought down bimanually and stays; a UDT springs back. Retractile needs yearly exams (10% secondary ascent), not surgery
  • PEx step 2: palpable or impalpable, true or ectopic. True UDT lies on the path of descent (abdominal 15%, inguinal 25%, suprascrotal 60%); all are palpable except abdominal. Ectopic lies off the path, most often superficial ectopic
  • Imaging: no role (poor sensitivity and specificity)

blocks.alt: Diagram of true and ectopic undescended testis positions
blocks.cap: True UDT lies along the line of descent (abdominal, inguinal, suprascrotal); ectopic testes sit off it (prepenile, superficial ectopic, transverse scrotal, femoral, perineal).

rows: Impaired after bilateral UDT (paternity 33-65%); unilateral has little effect
> 90% have an indirect inguinal hernia (large opening: bowel; small: hydrocele)
3-8x risk if untreated past puberty; surgery lowers it but still ~2x; higher position = higher risk; seminoma most common
blocks.lead: Orchidopexy for palpable and impalpable UDT, ideally at 6-18 months

blocks.html:
• Under anesthesia, first confirm it is not retractile
  • Palpable: inguinal orchidopexy. Non-palpable: laparoscopy to find it (intra-abdominal, vanishing, atrophic or peeping testis), then orchidopexy or orchiectomy

blocks.title: Bilateral non-palpable testes in a phenotypic male
blocks.html: An emergency: may be a virilized girl with congenital adrenal hyperplasia (↑ androgens in utero) at risk of salt wasting and adrenal crisis. Consult endocrinology; karyotype, Müllerian inhibiting substance, pelvic US. Also suspect a DSD with micropenis < 2 cm stretched in a term male, or unilateral UDT with proximal hypospadias; refer any bilateral UDT.

Acute scrotal pain
  • DDx: appendage torsion (#1), testicular torsion (#2), epididymo-orchitis (#3), trauma, hernia or hydrocele, tumour, referred pain (distal ureteral stone)
  • Torsion can present as lower abdominal pain: always examine the genitals in boys with abdominal pain

rows: Acute, severe, diffuse; unchanged by rest or activity
Early puberty (12-16 y); extravaginal form perinatal
Nausea and vomiting; horizontal lie; absent cremasteric reflex; erythema, edema, induration later; no dysuria or fever
No early erythema or swelling; blue dot sign (< 50%)
Fever, LUTS; erythema, induration, tenderness (hard to tell from torsion)
↓ or absent flow vs other side; heterogeneous = non-viable
Testis flow preserved; avascular ovoid nodule beside it
NSAIDs; resolves within a week (may worsen first); reassess if N/V
Empiric antibiotics; refer to find the cause

blocks.alt: Drawings of extravaginal and intravaginal testicular torsion
blocks.cap: Extravaginal torsion (A): the whole tunica vaginalis twists with the cord, perinatal and rare; intravaginal torsion (B): the cord twists inside the tunica, the bell clapper form of early puberty.

blocks.title: Torsion: the clock
blocks.html: Treat within 6 h to avoid orchiectomy; after 24 h, 80% of testes are dead. Don't delay for US if suspicion is high. Exploration fixes both testes (4% recurrence, 50% contralateral torsion risk); no effect on fertility or hormones. Manual detorsion (lateral, since 66% twist inward) only if no OR access: success 23-32%.

blocks.alt: Diagram of the testicular and epididymal appendages
blocks.cap: The appendages that can twist: appendix testis (Müllerian remnant, on the upper pole of the testis), appendix epididymis (Wolffian remnant), paradidymis and the vasa aberrantia of Haller.

blocks.html:
• Chemical epididymitis: no infection; urine refluxes up the vas (neurogenic bladder)
Phimosis
  • Physiological: normal non-retractile foreskin, retracts as the penis grows; 90% retractable by 3 y. Reassure, don't refer. Treat only recurrent true balanitis (not diaper rash): topical steroid BID x 6-8 wk with gentle retraction (70% effective)
  • Pathological: non-retractile from scarring (white ring), after recurrent balanitis or paraphimosis; steroids fail → circumcision
  • Paraphimosis: retracted foreskin with a tight band strangling the glans and blocking lymphatics: urologic emergency
  • PEx is key: scarring, balanitis, retractability (grade 0 fully retractable to 5); no investigations
  • Circumcision indications: BXO (balanitis xerotica obliterans), paraphimosis, recurrent balanitis, failed medical therapy; dorsal slit if urinary retention

rows: ↓ UTI in infants < 12 months; ↓ penile cancer (phimosis is a strong risk factor); ↓ HIV, STI, HPV
Complications 0.2-3%: bleeding, infection, glans injury, too much or too little skin removed, meatal stenosis (4%); poor cosmesis
blocks.lead: Neonatal circumcision (not routinely recommended by the Canadian Paediatric Society)

blocks.html:
Enuresis
  • Repeated loss of urine control; 7% of boys, 3% of girls at 5 y. Diagnose only > 5 y with ≥ 2 episodes a week for 3 months
  • Normal voiding: the pelvic floor holds until the right time, then relaxes as the detrusor contracts
  • Primary: never toilet trained; secondary: dry for 6 months, then relapse (neuro cause less likely)
  • Expected bladder capacity: children (age + 2) x 30 mL; infants 7 x weight (kg)

rows: Voiding postponement, vaginal trapping (low-volume wetting without urge), stressful events, bladder-bowel dysfunction (contracting the pelvic floor while the bladder fills → incomplete voiding, UTI, frequency, high-pressure voiding, constipation)
Small functional capacity, ↑ nighttime urine (OSA, evening fluids, diabetes insipidus, psychogenic polydipsia), heavy sleeper

As above, but rule out anatomic or neuro causes: overflow incontinence (stricture or neurogenic discoordination → high-pressure voiding), overactive bladder, ectopic ureter (continuous incontinence in girls)

blocks.html: • Renal impairment from high-pressure voiding or stasis: recurrent infection → renal scarring; trabeculated bladder that can scar and shrink

rows: Day, night or both; daily, intermittent or continuous; volume; postponement; LUTS; giggling, UTI, ↑ abdominal pressure; bowels (constipation); stressors, FHx, ADHD or anxiety; potty-training history; voiding diary
Back exam (spinal anomalies), genitals (meatal stenosis); uroflow: normal bell curve, intermittent = neurogenic, low flow + large residual = obstruction (post-void residual ≤ 20 mL); urinalysis
Renal bladder US for all (post-void: wall thickness, trabeculation, diverticula, dilation, rectal diameter); KUB (spine, stool); MRI spine if other imaging is abnormal

Most resolve: reassure. ↑ fluids (1 cup per year of age, max 8), timed frequent voids, treat constipation (prunes, PEG)
Postponement: timed voiding; vaginal trapping: legs apart or face the toilet
Small capacity: oxybutynin; heavy sleeper with normal capacity: bedwetting alarm
24 h output > 1-2 L: rule out DI, cut sugary and caffeinated drinks; nocturnal polyuria: DDAVP (symptomatic only) + evening fluid limit
Obstruction (stricture, meatal stenosis): surgery after spine cleared; continuous incontinence: surgery after confirming ectopic ureter

blocks.html:
Vesicoureteral reflux (VUR)
  • Normally the intramural ureter tunnels between mucosa and detrusor and is compressed shut as the bladder fills; in VUR the tunnel is short, so voiding pressure drives urine up to the kidney
  • Pressure transmitted to the kidney causes the damage; 1-2% of healthy children (more found by prenatal US); tends to resolve spontaneously (age, grade, bladder-bowel dysfunction)
  • A correctable cause of recurrent UTI: present in 30-50% of children with recurrent UTI. VUR + UTI → reflux nephropathy (dysplasia and scarring) → renal failure
  • Primary: congenital defect of the antireflux mechanism. Secondary: abnormal bladder or outlet (posterior urethral valves, neurogenic bladder, severe bladder-bowel dysfunction): check the back, treat the cause

rows: Abnormal US, 2 febrile UTIs (or a male neonate with a febrile UTI)
Needed to diagnose VUR: catheter fill and void; bladder outline (Christmas tree), grade I-V, urethra, residual, posterior urethral valves

blocks.alt: VUR grades I to V on VCUG diagrams
blocks.cap: VUR grades I-V: contrast reaches the ureter only (I), the non-dilated pelvis (II), mildly dilated pelvis and calyces (III), then progressively tortuous ureter and blunted calyces (IV-V).

rows: Low-dose daily antibiotic prophylaxis until resolution or toilet training
Bulking agent injected at the ureteric orifice

blocks.html:
Surgical indications
  • Breakthrough UTI on prophylaxis (the main one)
  • New scars on US or DMSA
  • Non-adherence to prophylaxis; febrile UTI after stopping antibiotics
  • Solitary kidney with high-grade VUR and scarring; persistent VUR after prolonged prophylaxis
  • Treat bladder-bowel dysfunction before surgery

blocks.title: Schulich Reviews
blocks.html:
• Appendage torsion = most common acute scrotum in children; blue-dot sign; conservative (NSAIDs)
  • UDT: most descend by 3–6 months; operate by 18 months; retractile testis stays down when brought down
  • Bilateral non-palpable testes in phenotypic male = emergency (CAH, salt wasting)
  • Circumcision for pathological phimosis, paraphimosis, recurrent balanitis
  • Enuresis: >5 y; secondary = dry ≥6 months then regressed

lectures.framing: Five common pediatric urology problems, each with one decision that matters: undescended testis (retractile or truly undescended, and when to operate), acute scrotal pain (torsion until proven otherwise), phimosis (physiological vs pathological), enuresis (what pattern, what capacity) and vesicoureteral reflux (who to image, prophylaxis vs surgery).
lectures.keypoints: UDT: 3% of boys, most descend by 3-6 months; no role for imaging; orchidopexy at 6-18 months; untreated past puberty → 3-8x cancer (seminoma). Bilateral non-palpable UDT in a phenotypic male = emergency (CAH girl, salt wasting). Scrotal pain: appendage torsion #1 (7-12 y, blue dot, NSAIDs); testicular torsion #2 (12-16 y, bell clapper, horizontal lie, absent cremasteric reflex, explore within 6 h, don't wait for US). Physiological phimosis: 90% retractable by 3 y, reassure; scarred (BXO) → circumcision. Enuresis: > 5 y; bladder capacity = (age + 2) x 30 mL; secondary = dry 6 months then relapse. VUR: US after a febrile UTI, VCUG to diagnose, DMSA for scars; prophylaxis for grade ≥ 3; breakthrough UTI → surgery (ureteric reimplant = gold standard).

lectures.name: Incontinence & Voiding Dysfunction
lectures.title: Incontinence and Voiding Dysfunction
lectures.framing: The bladder has a reservoir (detrusor) and an outlet (bladder neck and external sphincter). Voiding dysfunction comes from the nerves (neurogenic bladder), the reservoir or the outlet, and the history sorts symptoms into storage vs voiding. Treatment then follows the cause: BPH, stress, urge, neurogenic bladder or post-operative retention.
lectures.keypoints: Lesion level predicts the neurogenic bladder: suprapontine → overactivity (urgency ± incontinence); spinal cord → overactivity + detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia (can't void; back-pressure damages kidneys); peripheral (diabetes, alcohol, pelvic surgery) → areflexic bladder, can't void. Storage symptoms: frequency (normal 5-7/day), urgency, nocturia, incontinence; voiding symptoms: WISHED. Stress = leak with ↑ abdominal pressure → pelvic floor therapy, mid-urethral sling; urge = leak with urgency → anticholinergics (contraindicated in retention, untreated angle-closure glaucoma, gastric retention), mirabegron (β3), botox (5-10% retention). Weak stream from a weak detrusor and from outlet obstruction look the same: urodynamics tells them apart. Post-op retention: reverse causes, tamsulosin, repeat trial of void in 48 h. Refer all spinal cord injury patients.

blocks.html:
Reservoir and outlet
  • Reservoir = detrusor muscle; outlet = bladder neck + external urethral sphincter
  • In men the bladder neck is part of the prostate; in women the external sphincter matters more for continence
  • Neurogenic bladder can affect both reservoir and outlet; any CNS disease can change voiding

rows: Dementia, stroke, brain tumour, Parkinson's, MS, brain injury
Spinal cord injury, cauda equina syndrome, myelomeningocele
Urgency ± incontinence and inability to void (sphincter does not relax when the bladder contracts)
Diabetic neuropathy, alcohol, surgical injury (rectal cancer surgery, hysterectomy)

blocks.title: Patterns are not absolute
blocks.html: Lesions can be partial or severe and the body compensates, so these patterns do not always hold. DSD transmits high pressure back to the kidneys and can cause postrenal damage.

Drug and procedure details
  • Anticholinergics block bladder muscarinic receptors. Contraindicated in urinary retention, untreated acute angle-closure glaucoma and gastric retention. Side effects: dry mouth, constipation
  • Mirabegron (β3 agonist) relaxes the detrusor

Spinal cord injury
  • Loss of normal innervation → thick, non-compliant bladder → DSD → incontinence → kidney damage; check renal function with US and bloodwork
  • Also stones, UTIs, erectile dysfunction, autonomic dysreflexia
  • Goal: protect the kidneys, store urine at low pressure and empty voluntarily. Store: timed voiding, anticholinergics, botox, bladder augmentation. Empty: intermittent catheterisation (preferred), Foley or suprapubic catheter, reflex stimulation

blocks.html:
Why stones form
  • Diet: low intake of fluids, calcium, potassium (fruit/veg); high intake of salt and animal protein
  • Metabolic factors: idiopathic hypercalciuria (40%), hyperuricosuria (10%), hyperoxaluria (10%), hypocitraturia (8%), primary hyperparathyroidism (1%)
  • Investigate metabolic factors only for recurrent or multiple stones; a single stone former gets lifestyle advice

blocks.title: Hypercalcemia with stones
blocks.html: DDx: hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, vitamin D ± calcium intake, sarcoidosis, thiazides (which otherwise prevent calcium stones). Measure PTH; separate the rest by history and tests. Tx: remove the cause, IV saline + furosemide, bisphosphonates, parathyroidectomy if hyperPTH.

blocks.html:
Treatment
  • Conservative: analgesia (ketorolac or opioids), fluids, medical expulsive therapy: α-blocker (tamsulosin) relaxes ureteral smooth muscle
  • Surgical indications: severe unremitting pain, fever/UTI, renal failure (including solitary kidney or pre-existing dysfunction), occupation (pilots, bus drivers)

blocks.title: Fever plus an obstructing stone
blocks.html: High risk of rapid, potentially lethal sepsis. Antibiotics cannot reach an obstructed kidney, so it needs urgent drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy) to restore flow.

blocks.html:
Work-up for recurrent or multiple stones
  • Stone analysis and urine crystals
  • Imaging: location and opacity (opaque = calcium, lucent = uric acid)
  • Spot urine: urinalysis, pH, microscopy. Blood: calcium, uric acid, bicarbonate, PTH
  • 24-h urine: volume, pH, creatinine, oxalate, urate, citrate (inhibitor), K and urea
Specific prevention for calcium stones
  • Hyperoxaluria: low-oxalate diet and more calcium (binds oxalate in the gut)
  • Hyperuricosuria: low purine ± allopurinol
  • Hypocitraturia: potassium citrate
  • Hypercalciuria not responding to diet: thiazide (↓ urine calcium) or potassium citrate

lectures.framing: Kidney stones affect 10% of people and recur often. The page covers what stones are made of and why they form (diet, metabolic and secondary causes), the acute renal colic work-up and management (size decides who passes, infection decides who is drained), and prevention tailored to stone type.
lectures.keypoints: Calcium oxalate/phosphate = 80%, uric acid 15%, struvite 4%, cystine < 1%. Risk: low fluid, calcium and potassium intake; high salt and animal protein. Classic colic = unilateral severe flank pain radiating to the groin ± hematuria. Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard; uric acid stones are radiolucent on x-ray. Passage by size: < 4 mm 90%, 4-8 mm 50%, > 8 mm < 10%. Conservative care = analgesia (ketorolac), fluids, tamsulosin (MET). Fever/UTI with an obstructing stone = urgent drainage (stent or nephrostomy). Metabolic work-up (24-h urine) only for recurrent or multiple stones. Prevention: > 3 L fluid, normal calcium intake, low salt and protein; thiazide for hypercalciuria, K citrate for hypocitraturia, alkalinise for uric acid and cystine, remove infection and foreign bodies for struvite.

blocks.html: Cardiovascular disease is the #1 cause of death in patients on HD, PD or with a transplant, not kidney disease itself.

  • Bone disease on dialysis reflects vitamin D deficiency, secondary hyperparathyroidism and ↑ phosphate

lectures.framing: Stage 5 CKD (ESRD, GFR < 15) needs renal replacement, but not every eligible patient chooses dialysis. The page sets out when to dialyse (urgent vs elective), then compares the three options: hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis and transplantation.
lectures.keypoints: Urgent dialysis: seizures, coma, confusion, severe neuropathy, pericarditis, uncontrollable hyperkalemia, acidosis or fluid overload. Elective: anorexia, N/V, malnutrition, GFR < 5. ~20,000 Canadians on dialysis (80% HD, 20% PD), rising with diabetes. HD: 3-5 h three times weekly; AV fistula is the optimal access (graft clots, Permcath infects); needs anticoagulation; ultrafiltration by negative pressure. PD: peritoneum is the membrane, ultrafiltration by osmosis (hypertonic glucose); home-based, cheaper, more autonomy, protects residual function, similar survival, but peritonitis and more technique failure. Transplant = optimal RRT for survival and QOL. CVD is the #1 cause of death in ESRD, whatever the modality.
